articles.title: Italian taxpayers are paying millions to keep Russian yachts afloat
articles.summary: An expensive floating eyesore has marred views in the port of Trieste, northern Italy, for more than four years, and it is costing Italian taxpayers millions...
articles.body:
An expensive floating eyesore has marred views in the port of Trieste, northern Italy, for more than four years, and it is costing Italian taxpayers millions to maintain, the city's mayor says.

Russian oligarch Andrey Igorevich Melnichenko's "Sailing Yacht A," one of the world's largest sailing vessels and worth around $600 million, was in Trieste for maintenance in March 2022 when Russia's invasion of Ukraine led to widespread sanctions and seizures of Russian assets.

Among them was Melnichenko's 468-foot craft, once dubbed the "world's ugliest yacht" and known simply as "A" by locals who have grown to hate it. Designed by Philippe Starck, the superyacht features an outer surface that is ghostlike, its barely visible windows embedded in a shimmering armored steel frame. Its three rotating carbon masts are as tall as an eight-story palazzo, casting a silhouette that has by now become a fixture in the busy port where dozens of cruise ships dock each week.

In September 2025, Mayor Roberto Dipiazza raised the issue of who is paying for the yacht's mooring fees and maintenance in a public campaign, calling it a "disgrace," and threatening to sell it or sail it away. Dipiazza told CNN that the cost to keep the ship afloat, including paying for a 20-person crew, fuel to run the generators, specialized cleaning, security and insurance, amounts to around $30,000 a day – or nearly $11 million a year.

According to Italian law, a sequestered ship must be maintained and cannot be left to rust or sink. If and when sanctions against Melnichenko are lifted, he will have to pay back those costs to retrieve his vessel. "It will eventually cost him less to buy a new yacht than to pay back all we have spent," Dipazza said. "And where does that leave us? We could be paying for this monstrosity for years."

Melnichenko, a banker and industrialist whose fortune is estimated at around $20 billion, challenged the seizure of the yacht in the summer of 2022, arguing that the vessel was not directly owned by him, but instead a company called Valla Sails through a trust set up by his wife. The case was heard by a court in Rome in 2022 and eventually reached the Court of Justice of the European Union, which ruled in 2025 that Italy has the right to keep it sequestered – and with it, the obligation to maintain it.

Sailing Yacht A is not the only Russian yacht costing Italians money. In the Tuscan port of Marina di Carrara, the six-deck, 465-foot superyacht Scheherazade is docked behind high walls to keep it both safe and hidden from curious onlookers. While it is reportedly licensed to Rosneft executive Eduard Khudainatov, Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny credibly claimed it actually belongs to Russian President Vladimir Putin .

On August 28 of this year, it left the port heading north towards the Italian Rivieria, according to transponder signals recorded by Vessel Finder, heavily flanked by Italian security forces. It returned after ten hours of what a spokesperson for the Italian Sea Group, whose dock it is moored at, said were technical tests as part of its maintenance.

The superyacht, worth $700 million, has twin helipads among its many amenities and a swimming pool that converts to a dance floor, according to Superyacht Times.

The Scheherazade 's mooring contract had been paid through September, according to tax records seen by CNN. Italian Sea Group will not say who paid for, or who is now paying for, those mooring costs. Since it was sequestered, Tuscan taxpayers have paid more than $15 million for the skeleton crew, some of whom are British and others Russian, which switches out several times a year, according to local press reports. A film crew that tried to approach the vessel last year was chased away by drones and water cannon.

Additional costs include the security to make sure no one gets close – and that it doesn't set sail while sequestered.

Among the other vessels that Italy is paying to keep is the Lady M , a sleek 210-foot superyacht owned by Alexei Mordashov, a Putin associate and majority shareholder in Severstal, Russia's largest steel and mining company. Forbes puts Mordashov's net worth at nearly $37 billion. Lady M is sequestered in Imperia, and has cost Italian taxpayers around $2 million so far, Matteo Bonjean, vice director of the port of Marina di Imperia, told Forbes.

The 126-foot superyacht Lena , owned by Gennady Timchenko, another Putin ally, is being maintained nearby.

All of the sequestered vessels have crews that maintain the yachts, paid for by the Italian government. Other costs include the use of air conditioning to prevent mold from growing inside.

Italy is by no means the only country stuck with costs for sequestered yachts in Europe. Germany has the $800 million Dilbar , owned at one time by the sister of sanctioned Russian magnate Alisher Usmanov. France is paying to keep the sanctioned oligarch Igor Sechin's Amore Ver a, and Spain maintains the Tango , owned by sanctioned Russian oligarch Viktor Vekselberg.

Gibraltar was able to auction off Russian steel magnate Dmitry Pumpyansky's 236-foot Axioma for some $37.5 million, according to Reuters. The United States has sold several vessels, including the Amadea, owned by twice-sanctioned Russian politician Suleiman Kerimov.

Not all countries choose to pay upkeep if their national laws don't require it. Sanctioned Russian Andrey Guryev's massive 353-foot Luminosity , sequestered in Montenegro, has been left to rust and rot, according to images posted on social media by Benetti Yachts, which built the ship. Montenegro tried to sell the yacht in 2024 for €135 million, but the sale was ultimately blocked and the yacht continues to languish in the Porto Montenegro marina in Tivat.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has been a strong supporter of maintaining sanctions against Russian oligarchs tied to Putin, warning the Italian Senate last month that any softening or deal making with Moscow was "a very risky choice." Many others, like Trieste mayor Dipiazza, feel that taxpayers should not have to pay for the upkeep of oligarchs' toys.

articles.title: Deadly shooting rocks California coastal community, leaving 2 dead, 2 injured
articles.summary: Authorities are investigating what led to the deadly early-morning shooting near Moss Landing State Beach that left two people dead and two others injured.
articles.body: Two people were killed and two others injured in a shooting near a California beach early Monday, authorities said. The Monterey County Sheriff's Office said deputies, California State Parks personnel and California Highway Patrol officers responded to reports of gunfire along Jetty Road in Moss Landing just before 2 a.m. Deputies found two people who were pronounced dead at the scene, the sheriff's office said. A third person who had been shot arrived at a local hospital. That person's condition was unknown. ONE DEAD, 6 INJURED AFTER GUNFIRE ERUPTS AT UNSANCTIONED CALIFORNIA PARTY THAT DREW HUNDREDS: SHERIFF A fourth person was taken from the scene to a hospital with injuries that were not considered life-threatening, authorities said. The identities of the two people killed were being withheld pending forensic examinations and notification of their families. "This is a tragic incident that has resulted in the loss of two lives," Monterey County Sheriff Tina M. Nieto said in a statement. "Our detectives are working to establish the circumstances surrounding what occurred. We ask anyone who may have information, regardless of how insignificant it may seem, to come forward and assist with this investigation." SHOOTING AT FLORIDA BEACH 'TEEN TAKEOVER' LEAVES 17-YEAR-OLD HOSPITALIZED WITH GUNSHOT WOUND California State Parks Police closed Jetty Road and Moss Landing State Beach at the request of the sheriff's office as the investigation continued. "There is no active threat to the Moss Landing Community at this time," the sheriff's office said. Authorities have not said what led to the shooting. "This remains an active investigation and additional information will be released as it becomes available," the sheriff's office said. State Sen. John Laird called the shooting an "unspeakable horror" and offered his condolences to those affected. FLORIDA WOMAN, 70, OPENS FIRE INSIDE PORT ORANGE POLICE DEPARTMENT LOBBY, CHIEF SAYS "Over the weekend, there were numerous reports of shooting deaths across the country. This unspeakable horror has also hit home on the Central Coast, with reports of multiple fatalities just after midnight today in Moss Landing," Laird said in a statement. "The pain and suffering of all those impacted is impossible to measure and my heart goes out to everyone. Thank you to the Monterey County Sheriff and team for its management of this devastating situation." articles.title: Russia plotting 'massive strike' during midterms, Zelenskyy warns, urges US to stop Putin
articles.summary: Zelenskyy says Russia plans a massive attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure while the world watches Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections unfold.
articles.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Monday that Russia is preparing a "massive attack" on Ukraine centered on Tuesday's midterm elections in the United States, accusing Moscow of seeking to exploit the historical vote to unleash strikes while the world's attention is elsewhere. The Ukrainian leader's warning came as voters prepared to decide which party controls Congress, a result that could also influence Washington's future response to Russian President Vladimir Putin's almost five-year war in Ukraine. In a post on X, Zelenskyy went on to urge the Trump administration to increase pressure on Moscow, warning that Russia could exploit the elections to target Ukraine's battered energy infrastructure and supply routes. DRONE STRIKE SINKS SHIP IN NATO WATERS AS ZELENSKYY WARNS OF LOOMING ‘MASSIVE STRIKE’ "We have intel that Russia is preparing a new massive attack on our country – primarily targeting energy and logistics," Zelenskyy said in his nightly address. "The assumption is basically that tomorrow the world will be watching the American midterms, and what is happening here in Ukraine, along with our difficulties with air defense and Patriot missiles, will be overlooked." Zelenskyy's warning came hours after Russian forces struck a school being used to distribute humanitarian aid in Komyshuvakha, a settlement in southeastern Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region. At least 26 people, including police officers and first responders, were killed, five others were injured and others remained missing, according to the Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda. ZELENSKYY PRESSURES US AND EUROPE FOR MORE 'AIR DEFENSE' ASSISTANCE AMID ONGOING WAR WITH RUSSIA In his X post, Zelenskyy urged the U.S. and its allies to warn Putin that continued attacks on Ukraine would bring serious economic consequences. "We need signals from the world to Russia that will make them feel that terror is no good, that it will bring no gains, and that as long as this war continues, their oil will burn, and they will not be able to make money doing business with the world," Zelenskyy warned. "We must not play games with Russia's oil or gas revenues," he added. "We must put pressure on Russia in such a way that it has no alternative but to end this war. America can do this." TRUMP ANNOUNCES IMMEDIATE ENERGY CEASEFIRE BETWEEN RUSSIA AND UKRAINE President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has sought to negotiate an end to the war with the help of special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, both of whom have been involved in diplomatic efforts with Moscow. Zelenskyy told Fox News in a Sunday interview that Ukraine would suspend strikes on Russian oil refineries for a month if Washington provided Patriot missile interceptors during the same period, potentially opening the door to diplomacy. The State Department approved the potential sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 interceptor missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1 billion, according to Reuters. The proposed sale could provide a significant boost to Ukraine's air defenses if finalized, although the delivery timeline is uncertain. TRUMP SAYS US WILL LET UKRAINE MAKE PATRIOT MISSILES IN MAJOR POLICY SHIFT On Monday, Ukraine also accused Moscow of exploiting a U.S.-backed humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky, in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, to strengthen Russian military positions. Nearly 800 people were evacuated during the six-day humanitarian pause, according to first lady Melania Trump, with the White House clarifying that she helped broker the arrangement. Ukraine's General Staff accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian pause to rotate troops, reinforce their defenses and improve battlefield logistics. "Under the ceasefire introduced for the humanitarian operation in Oleshky, units of the Defence Forces of Ukraine ensured that the ceasefire was observed and acted exclusively within the framework of the agreements reached," the General Staff said in a statement on X. articles.title: Who are the victims of the deadly Florida jet crash?
articles.summary: Sunday's crash killed all nine people aboard, including a tech entrepreneur and his young family, as well as the 20-year-old copilot.
articles.body:
Nine people have been killed after a small jet crashed and exploded in Florida on Sunday.

The Learjet 60 was bound for the Bahamas from Austin when it nosedived into a multi-lane highway.

The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating whether ice and turbulence contributed to the crash, and whether human error played a role.

Here is what we know so far about the victims.

The Texas tech entrepreneur, his wife Helen Sharp and their two children, Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2, were all killed in the crash, according to a joint statement from some of the families of those killed.

Their family described them as "devoted parents" and said their children were "the light of their lives".

"Helen and Adam were the love affair that will last forever. Their warmth, generosity and gift for making people feel welcome touched so many lives," the statement reads.

On his LinkedIn page, Robinson described himself as the founder and CEO of RB2B and Retention.com, and the CEO of Moltsets.

He previously worked at global financial services business Lehman Brothers and the banking group Barclays.

The BBC has contacted the companies for a statement.

Fellow tech entrepreneur Jesse Ouellette posted on LinkedIn about Robinson's death, saying he had helped him when he was building his company.

"He became a friend and someone I saw eye to eye with on how to build software companies," wrote Ouellette.

"He could disagree with you about almost anything, and somehow you'd walk away liking him even more."

Copilot in deadly Florida jet crash identified in reports as 20-year-old

Robinson's last post on the networking site was on Sunday, about a debate he and Ouellette had scheduled for the following week.

Helen Sharp, meanwhile, was an artist, according to media reports.

Her father, Dudley Sharp, told the Florida news site The Palm Beach Post that news his family had been on the plane was "quite a blow".

"We had a daughter, her husband and two grandchildren on the plane," he said.

Rachel Reed, Charmi Fehr and Anita Maria Cetina

Reed, Fehr and Cetina were also travelling aboard the jet with Robinson Sharp and their children.

Reed and Fehr were described in the joint family statement as "full of joy and adventure".

"They loved their people fiercely, fully and without hesitation. From the moment they met, they were all in on each other and the life they were building," it added.

It was not immediately clear what their relationship was with Robinson and Sharp.

The statement said Cetina "cared for Emma and Charlie with tenderness and devotion, and she was truly part of the family".

It added: "She showed us a legacy of unconditional love and devotion."

Gregory, 55, has been identified as the pilot of the plane, according to East Coast Jets, a private charter company where Gregory used to work.

"We are deeply saddened to learn that Captain Jeff Gregory was among those who lost their lives in yesterday's tragic aviation accident in Palm Beach," a spokesperson for the company said in a statement on Monday.

Jeff worked for East Coast Jets "briefly" in 2016 and 2017, the spokesperson said.

US media has identified Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, as the copilot of the plane. She earned her pilot's licence when she was 17.

Filgueiras's mother, Camila Corteleti, confirmed to US media that her daughter had died in the fireball.

Corteleti told the New York Times: "She loved the freedom. It was completely different seeing the world from the top."

In a 2023 interview with a local news affiliate of CBS News, Filgueiras spoke proudly of receiving her pilot's licence while still a senior in high school.

"I like being different than everyone," she said. "Some people think that it's weird that I can fly planes, but I can't drive a car, I mean I can but, a lot of people think it's funny."

articles.title: Newspaper headlines: Mahmood's 'Duty of care' or 'climbdown' and 'The new cold war'
articles.summary: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's revision of settlement plans for migrant care workers features prominently in Tuesday's papers.
articles.body:
"The new Cold War", is how the Metro describes the sabotage of supermarket freezers across Europe. The paper says "stunned" staff turned up for morning shifts to see floors flooded and tonnes of frozen food ruined. The Financial Times reports that freezers in shops across Sweden "were turned up as high as 55 Celsius". According to the Sun , the UK is now "on alert " with "fears of a similar attack" on Britain.

Under the headline "duty of care", the Daily Mirror leads on what it calls the home secretary's "rethink" of immigration reforms. Hundreds of thousands of those in the care sector will now be able to claim indefinite leave to remain in the UK after five years, instead of the 15 originally proposed. The Times says Mahmood "bowed to pressure" from cabinet colleagues and Labour MPs. The Daily Mail calls her statement a climbdown ; the Guardian describes it as a softening of the original plans.

The prospect of a formal apology from the UK for its role in the slave trade has led the Daily Express editorial to call for the prime minister to learn "when to put a sock in it". The paper says Andy Burnham's "unwise intervention" has made the King's job at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting "more difficult". The Daily Mirror 's Darren Lewis writes that Burnham is "right to be open" on the issue, but the Daily Mail 's leader says its "yet another example" of the PM's "pathological inability to say no".

According to the Sun , the prime minister also "flew into a major storm" over his travel arrangements to Antigua for the Commonwealth meeting. A government aircraft took off from Stansted with officials on board before being diverted to Manchester to pick up Andy Burnham and his wife. The Conservatives say the jet was "the world's most expensive Uber". Downing Street says the diversion was value for money.

"America's crossroads" is how the i Paper tees up the US midterm elections. The Guardian calls them a "referendum" on Donald Trump's second presidency and "a chance for opponents to rein in his untrammelled power". The Daily Mirror offers its readers a prediction - that the president's Republican party are "all set for a trumping".

images.caption: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's revision of settlement plans for migrant care workers features prominently in Tuesday's papers. Mahmood had planned to make foreign care workers already in the UK wait 15 years to qualify for permanent settlement. Instead she has "softened plans" to help the struggling sector, the Daily Mirror reports.

articles.title: Iran war live: US carries out ‘defensive’ strikes in Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: US forces target Iranian positions in the Strait of Hormuz in “defensive” strikes following missile threats.
articles.body:
The United States military has carried out “limited defensive” strikes against Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz following surface-to-air missile threats against US assets, according to the Associated Press.

US Vice President JD Vance says Washington has made “progress” in indirect peace talks with Iran, while Tehran insists the US must lift its naval blockade and meet its demands before any agreement is reached.

articles.summary: O blog comemora dez anos firme no compromisso de combater a visão negativa que ainda se tem do envelhecimento
articles.body:
A data de hoje tem um significado muito especial para mim: o blog Longevidade: modo de usar está completando dez anos! No dia 3 de novembro de 2016, a coluna de estreia se intitulava “Infância e adolescência foram reinventadas. Agora é a vez da velhice”, e essa era a abertura do texto: “Normalmente, quando digo minha idade, 58 anos, recebo em troca um ‘não parece!’. O que mais chama a atenção no cumprimento é a negação que ele embute: por que não posso parecer ter 58 anos? Aliás, por que não posso ter a minha idade? E, finalmente, por que envelhecer ainda é tabu?”. Uma década depois, com quatro livros lançados na área de longevidade, sou uma idosa e militante apaixonada pela causa.

Idosa dançando: geração que derrubou dogmas na juventude não está nem um pouco disposta a ter um papel secundário na velhice — Foto: Age without limits

Para a coluna, resolvi compartilhar alguns ensinamentos da psicóloga Cristiane Novaes, doutora em Saúde Pública e Meio Ambiente pela Escola Nacional de Saúde Pública da Fundação Oswaldo Cruz e professora associada da Universidade Federal do Estado do Rio de Janeiro (UNIRIO). Ela ministrou uma palestra no GeriatRio 2026, realizado em outubro, mostrando como as mudanças climáticas afetam duramente os mais velhos, mas também foi bastante assertiva sobre a importância da resiliência para lidarmos com os desafios do envelhecimento: “Não se trata de otimismo barato, é uma resposta psicobiológica mensurável que abranda o impacto do estresse sistêmico crônico”, afirmou.

Novaes enumerou os principais desafios atrelados à velhice – declínio físico, isolamento, sentimento de inutilidade, luto pela perda de entes queridos e percepção da proximidade da morte –, mas fez um contraponto com o que chamou de estratégias de adaptação: “uma busca intencional por aceitação, o desejo por aprendizado, a reconstrução de novos significados de vida”.

Na sua avaliação, o envelhecimento traz “uma negociação constante e diária para conciliar perdas, em qualquer esfera, com o esforço consciente de adaptação”. E algumas ferramentas de resiliência podem ser valiosas:

Tecnologia: o domínio tecnológico atua como uma ponte vital contra o isolamento.

Atitude positiva: reinterpretação contínua das limitações impostas e valorização das capacidades remanescentes.

Espiritualidade: âncora existencial profunda que funciona como um mecanismo interno de enfrentamento, oferecendo propósito e paz diante da finitude incontrolável.

De resiliência, certamente entendemos, e assino embaixo do que escrevi há dez anos: “A velhice terá que ser reinventada por quem está chegando lá, essa geração que derrubou dogmas e é dona do próprio nariz, e que não está nem um pouco disposta a ter um papel secundário no cenário mundial”. Acredito que minha geração tem a missão de combater a visão negativa do envelhecimento. Também acredito que venho honrando o que prometi fazer, como mostra o encerramento do texto de estreia: “A proposta dessa coluna é ambiciosa e, ao mesmo tempo, otimista: ser um fórum sobre o curso de nossas vidas, tratando de todos os temas relacionados com a maturidade. Não tenho a menor pretensão de fazer isso sozinha. Desde já convido todos a contribuir com esta discussão. E vamos à luta!”. Agradeço de coração a todos que vêm me acompanhando nessa jornada.

Restaurante Comunitário DJ Jamaika fecha por três meses para manutenção em Ceilândia — Foto: Agência Brasília/reprodução

O Restaurante Comunitário de Ceilândia Centro (DJ Jamaika) vai fechar temporariamente a partir desta terça-feira (3) para passar por obras de manutenção. A previsão é que a unidade fique três meses sem atendimento ao público.

A Sedes informou ainda que não haverá transporte durante o café da manhã nem aos fins de semana .

Segundo a Sedes-DF, após a manutenção, o Restaurante Comunitário DJ Jamaika passará a funcionar todos os dias, inclusive domingos e feriados, com oferta de três refeições:

Atualmente, a unidade funciona de segunda-feira a sábado e oferece apenas café da manhã e almoço.

A reforma prevê a reorganização das áreas de produção e armazenamento de alimentos, o remanejamento de equipamentos e a instalação de uma terceira câmara fria.

De acordo com a secretaria, as mudanças buscam ampliar a capacidade de produção de refeições e melhorar o atendimento à população.

“Pedimos a compreensão da população pelo fechamento temporário, mas estamos trabalhando para aprimorar e ampliar o serviço para a comunidade”, afirmou o secretário substituto de Desenvolvimento Social, Rafael Rodrigues.

articles.title: Por que as eleições nos EUA são sempre em uma terça-feira de novembro | G1
articles.standfirst: Escolha da data tem raízes nas práticas agrícolas e culturais da sociedade norte-americana do século 19.
articles.summary: Escolha da data tem raízes nas práticas agrícolas e culturais da sociedade norte-americana do século 19.
articles.body:
As eleições de meio de mandato nos Estados Unidos vão seguir uma tradição do século 19 já conhecida dos norte-americanos: serão em novembro e em uma terça-feira . Neste ano, estão marcadas para esta terça-feira (3).

▶️ Contexto: Diferentemente do Brasil, o Congresso dos Estados Unidos é renovado parcialmente a cada dois anos. Quando ocorrem na metade do mandato presidencial, essas eleições são chamadas de midterms, ou eleições de meio de mandato.

Os deputados norte-americanos têm mandatos de dois anos, enquanto os senadores, de seis.

Com isso, a cada dois anos, o país renova toda a Câmara dos Representantes e cerca de um terço do Senado .

Sendo assim, desta vez, estarão em disputa todas as 435 cadeiras da Câmara e 35 das 100 cadeiras do Senado.

A data escolhida para a votação começou com a uma lei aprovada pelo Congresso dos Estados Unidos em 1845. O costume vem do contexto agrícola em que o país vivia no século 19, quando a lei foi aprovada.

Naquela época, os congressistas resolveram escolher novembro como o mês das eleições para coincidir com o período pós-colheita .

Os parlamentares também levaram em consideração o clima. Novembro marca o outono norte-americano, com temperaturas amenas , mas sem frio intenso.

👉 Essa decisão facilitava a participação dos eleitores que viviam majoritariamente nas zonas rurais.

Eleitores votam durante a votação antecipada antes das eleições de meio de mandato em Cleveland, Ohio, EUA, 1º de novembro de 2026. — Foto: Shannon Stapleton/Reuters

Uma lei aprovada nos Estados Unidos em 1845 estabeleceu que as eleições presidenciais fossem feitas sempre na primeira terça-feira após a primeira segunda-feira de novembro . Em 1872, o Congresso aprovou estender a regra às eleições para a Câmara dos Representantes, a partir de 1876. Posteriormente, a disputa pelo Senado também foi incluída.

A escolha impede que as eleições ocorram em 1º de novembro, que é o Dia de Todos os Santos.

No caso deste ano, a primeira segunda-feira de novembro é dia 2 . Sendo assim, a eleição foi marcada para o dia 3.

Nas últimas eleições de meio de mandato, em 2022, o dia 1º de novembro caiu em uma terça-feira . Sendo assim, o pleito foi marcado apenas para o dia 8, após a primeira segunda-feira do mês.

Historicamente, a terça-feira foi escolhida para atender aspectos culturais da sociedade norte-americana do século 19 : o fim de semana era geralmente reservado para atividades religiosas , e a quarta-feira era utilizada em áreas rurais para o mercado .

Naquela época, os eleitores precisavam viajar longas distâncias para comparecer aos centros de votação, sendo que muitos saíam de casa com um dia de antecedência para chegar a tempo.

Com isso em mente, os congressistas optaram pela terça-feira, permitindo que os eleitores iniciassem suas viagens na segunda-feira, votassem no dia seguinte e retornassem a tempo para o mercado.

Nos últimos anos, alguns movimentos surgiram nos Estados Unidos pedindo para que as eleições aconteçam no fim de semana. Eles argumentam que a sociedade mudou, e o pleito em um sábado ou domingo contribuiria para o comparecimento de trabalhadores, tendo em vista que o voto no país não é obrigatório.

Urna eletrônica brasileira — Foto: Giuliano Gomes/PR Press

No Brasil, a Constituição Federal determina que o primeiro turno da eleição presidencial aconteça sempre no primeiro domingo de outubro.

Se houver necessidade de segundo turno, o pleito será marcado para o último domingo do mesmo mês.

A exceção foi para as eleições de 2020, quando o calendário eleitoral acabou sendo atrasado por causa da pandemia de Covid-19.

O Código Eleitoral brasileiro também estabelece que o dia das eleições seja considerado feriado nacional. Essa norma existe para facilitar o acesso da população aos locais de votação.

articles.title: Sanfoneiro cego toca na mesma rua há 46 anos e busca sonho | G1
articles.standfirst: Stefano, de 53 anos, enfrenta problemas de saúde, vive das contribuições de quem passa pelo local e sonha em levar as próprias músicas para o streaming.
articles.summary: O sanfoneiro de Campinas Stefano toca todos os dias na Rua 13 de Maio enquanto sonha em levar sua música ao streaming.
articles.body:
Há mais de quatro décadas, o som da sanfona de Walter Baptista Junior, conhecido como Stefano, faz parte da rotina de quem passa pela Rua 13 de Maio, no Centro de Campinas (SP).

Aos 53 anos, o músico com deficiência visual segue ocupando o mesmo ponto onde começou a tocar ainda criança, aos 7 anos. Entre as notas do acordeão e o movimento apressado dos pedestres, construiu uma história marcada pela música, pela persistência e pelo sonho de alcançar novos públicos.

A rotina começa cedo, longe dali. Por volta das 6h, Stefano sai de casa, em Monte Mor (SP), levando a sanfona, uma caixa para receber contribuições e uma bolsa. Com o auxílio de uma bengala, faz o trajeto até Campinas para mais um dia de apresentações.

Nascido na capital paulista e registrado em Campinas, o músico cego cresceu entre os sons e o movimento do comércio popular. Na infância, chegava acompanhado da mãe e, depois, das irmãs. Aos 16 anos, começou a fazer o caminho sozinho.

Segundo ele, o início não foi fácil. Stefano conta que, quando era mais novo, ouvia críticas de quem passava pela rua.

"Ah, eu não sabia tocar direito, fazia barulho, ainda levava carão das turmas. Quando completei 16 anos, completei o ritmo certo", lembra.

Hoje, as apresentações seguem até as 14h. Entre uma melodia e outra, o músico também arranca sorrisos com uma corneta de brinquedo que costuma carregar.

Ao longo dos anos, a música permaneceu, mas muita coisa mudou ao redor. Há cerca de seis anos, Stefano precisou se adaptar novamente à rotina sem a companhia das irmãs, que se casaram.

Durante um período, também dividiu o ponto com o irmão, conhecido como "Branquinho", que morreu em decorrência de um câncer.

Walter Baptista Junior, de 53 anos, toca há mais de 40 anos na Rua 13 de Maio, no Centro de Campinas (SP) — Foto: Bianca Garutti/g1

A relação de Stefano com a música começou com um acordeão de oito baixos, um presente do avô. Foi com o instrumento que descobriu, ainda criança, uma paixão que o acompanharia por toda a vida.

Sem frequentar escolas de música, aprendeu as primeiras canções com o tio. O restante veio da prática, da curiosidade e dos ouvidos atentos. Nota por nota, desenvolveu uma técnica própria, que aperfeiçoou ao longo dos anos .

"Se você tiver acordeão, você tem que pegar todo santo dia, não pode parar um dia, senão você esquece tudo de novo. Até você pegar a prática. Aí, depois que você pegou a prática, já era", explica.

A habilidade não ficou restrita à sanfona. Stefano também toca teclado e gaita de ponto. No repertório, mistura músicas populares, como "Mulher Chorona", e canções religiosas, como o Hino 15.

Stefano com a sanfona que ganhou do avô — Foto: Bianca Garutti/g1

São mais de 40 anos no mesmo endereço, embalando o vai e vem de milhares de pessoas. Mas, apesar de fazer parte da paisagem sonora do Centro, Stefano conta que nem sempre se sente visto por quem passa .

O músico diz sentir falta de reconhecimento e, sobretudo, de algo mais simples: uma conversa .

"Ah, até hoje ninguém falou comigo ainda não. É difícil, sério, é difícil. Nem dá atenção, não fala nada", desabafa.

A rotina também exige cuidados com a saúde. Stefano tem diabetes e cirrose hepática e precisa de acompanhamento médico regular . Por isso, reserva os fins de semana para descansar e recuperar as energias antes de voltar à rua.

"Sábado e domingo é descanso. Já tô com problema de saúde. Se eu vir direto, eu vou me acabar desse jeito", conta.

O dinheiro recebido durante as apresentações ajuda a pagar as despesas de casa. Mas, segundo ele, as contribuições nem sempre são suficientes para acompanhar o aumento do custo de vida.

"Eu vou comprar as coisas em casa. Nem dá ainda, porque as coisas estão caras", lamenta.

O sonho de estar nos palcos e no streaming

Depois de mais de quatro décadas tocando para quem cruza a Rua 13 de Maio, Stefano ainda sonha em alcançar plateias maiores. Quer se apresentar em grandes shows e fazer com que sua música chegue a pessoas que nunca passaram pelo Centro de Campinas.

Um dos maiores desejos dele é disponibilizar as próprias composições nas plataformas de streaming. A dificuldade, segundo ele, está em descobrir como transformar esse sonho em realidade.

"Eu queria me publicar mais no Spotify mesmo, né? Que lá todo mundo ouve. Não sei como faz. Se alguém fizesse para mim, eu agradeceria muito essa pessoa", conta.

*Estagiária sob supervisão de Gabriella Ramos.

articles.title: Race Course, Savda Ghevra: Historic Delhi mosque fights for its future
articles.summary: Authorities have razed hundreds of houses in a neighbourhood in central Delhi, saying they were built on government land.
articles.body:
In the heart of Delhi, a short distance from the Indian prime minister's residence, a small mosque stands amid piles of rubble. Its pale walls and pointed arches remain intact, its courtyard still lined with green-and-white tiles.

But the people who gave life to the place are gone.

Mohammad Wasim, 50, points across the rubble to the spot where his house once stood.

"My father was married there, and, decades later, so was my daughter," says Wasim, a driver.

Wasim and his family were among hundreds of people who lived around the mosque in a patchwork of modest homes tucked between military compounds, exclusive clubs and sprawling bungalows in Race Course, one of the Indian capital's wealthiest and most heavily guarded neighbourhoods. Many of them had lived here for generations, working as drivers, cleaners and gardeners in the wealthy houses around them.

On 7 October, the authorities demolished their houses across three settlements, saying they had been built illegally on government land. They also raised security concerns because of the houses' proximity to military installations. Some 717 families were relocated to Savda Ghevra, a colony nearly 31 miles away, on the city's outskirts.

Residents had challenged the evictions in the Delhi High Court, arguing that moving so far from their jobs, schools and communities would upend their lives. But in August, the court allowed the relocation, accepting the government's security concerns and noting that alternative housing had been provided.

Only the mosque and a nearby Hindu temple were left standing. But their water and electricity supplies were cut off that day, and access to the compound has since been restricted. Worshippers are generally turned away at the gates, though some are occasionally allowed through after pleading with guards.

The government says it owns the land on which the mosque stands, but mosque authorities say it was registered in 1977 as waqf property - land or buildings set aside under Islamic law for religious or charitable purposes - and is listed as a heritage structure. The Delhi Waqf Board says it is nearly 300 years old, though other estimates put its age at 125-150 years.

The board has written to the authorities seeking restoration of the mosque's water and electricity and raising concerns about its future. Separately, a worshipper has petitioned the high court over restrictions on prayers and fears that the mosque could be demolished.

On 29 October, the government told the court it would take no action against the mosque for four weeks while considering the board's objections. It opposed restoring access for prayers, citing safety concerns during demolition work, a position disputed by the worshippers' lawyer. The court declined to intervene and scheduled another hearing for 16 December.

While the mosque's future remains uncertain, for those who once lived around it, the question now is what can be salvaged of the lives they built there.

Wasim still returns to the mosque to pray when he can, though guards sometimes turn him away. On a recent afternoon, he was among just four or five worshippers inside. A generator chugged loudly outside, supplying electricity after the power had been cut off.

"Our hearts and entire lives are tied to this place," he says. "How can we let it go, when our childhood was spent playing here?"

Rekha, a widow, remembers the colony with longing. She washed dishes in nearby homes, raised her family and performed seva (voluntary service) at the local temple.

To her, the word rehabilitation seems painfully inadequate: "How can a life built over decades be uprooted and planted somewhere else?" she asks.

Since the move, she has lost the work she depended on. Her 19-year-old son is struggling to find a job. She has been allotted a third-floor apartment but climbing stairs is painful because of a metal rod in her leg after an operation.

"I may have a house but my home was snatched away."

Critics say these experiences are part of a longer history of displacement in Delhi, where working-class communities have repeatedly been pushed to the city's distant edges because they lack documents proving legal ownership of land they have lived on for decades.

"Relocation disconnects them from both jobs and networks, resulting in livelihood and income loss," urban researcher Mukta Naik told the BBC.

As families scatter in search of work, she says, the informal support systems they once relied on become harder to rebuild.

"This leaves families to fend for themselves," she says.

The Delhi government's housing agency, the local municipal council and the central government's land office did not respond to requests for comment.

Savda Ghevra was established in 2006 on farmland near Delhi's border with Haryana state, to house families displaced from elsewhere in the city.

The first arrivals found little more than bare plots, without roads, running water or electricity. Over time, they built homes, opened shops and fought for basic services. By the early 2020s, an estimated 50,000 people lived here , having made a neighbourhood out of a place they had little choice but to inhabit.

Now the families from Race Course have begun the same slow work.

They have traded the lush tree-lined avenues of central Delhi for rows of nearly identical concrete blocks, with open fields stretching beyond. Life is going on, but much of what sustained these families remains on the other side of the city.

Every day, Babloo leaves home at 5am to take his children by metro to their old school in central Delhi, changing trains three times along the way. He waits out the six hours until classes finish at a tea stall outside his former neighbourhood. When he has work his wife makes the journey.

Their new home is too far away, he says, to return between the school runs. By the time the family reaches Savda Ghevra, it is around 4pm.

Babloo once worked at a club in Race Course. He has now found work in Meerut, a town to the north-east of Delhi. Residents knew they might have to leave, he says, but they hoped they would be relocated somewhere close enough to continue their jobs and their children's schooling.

The government says suitable apartments were unavailable closer to Race Course. In court, it cited Savda Ghevra's schools, dispensaries and transport links as evidence that the area could accommodate the displaced families.

But the presence of these facilities offers little reassurance to Naeem Khan, 63. His two grandsons have hearing and speech disabilities and need specialised care and schooling that he says are unavailable in the area.

The move has also scattered Naeem's family. One son and a divorced daughter share his tiny one-room apartment, while his two other sons had to move elsewhere due to lack of space.

"We have been thrown 20 years backward," he says.

The distance has been especially costly for women. Naik says childcare responsibilities, transport costs and safety concerns make long commutes to work particularly difficult for them.

At Race Course, the wealth surrounding the settlements offered small but vital ways to earn money - dishes to wash, gardens to tend, discarded bottles to collect and sell.

Akhtari, an elderly widow, collected mineral-water bottles for about 100 rupees (about $1.05; £0.80) a day and dried leftover rotis, or flatbreads, to sell as cattle feed.

Now even these modest sources of income have disappeared.

"Everyone living here was evicted; everyone is poor, broken, and struggling themselves," Akhtari says. "Who will hire someone else for housework?"

At Race Course, when she had nothing, the mosque's imam or a neighbour might give her money for flour. Her neighbours checked on her. In the new apartment, she has a roof over her head, but few people to fall back on.

She has begun to worry about what will happen if she falls ill.

"If I collapse and die inside, no one will even know," she says. " Hopefully someone will break down the door and find me."

articles.title: Indicted ICE officer had been on the job a little over a year as Trump’s hiring surge comes under scrutiny
articles.summary: Mario Alberto Morales was released on bond following his indictment on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.
articles.body: ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales turned himself in Monday after being indicted last week in connection with running over a man who was on foot. The case has put Morales’ work record under scrutiny and called attention to the administration’s hiring surge last year to fill in immigration enforcement posts. Morales, 33, was released on a $30,000 bond after a hearing before District Judge Matthew Peneguy in Harris County, Texas. He had been indicted Friday on a second-degree felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. The case has escalated criticism of the administration’s attempt to quickly increase the ranks of ICE officers to fulfill President Donald Trump’s mass deportation pledge, just as voters are heading to the polls for midterm elections. Last year, several Department of Homeland Security officials told NBC News some of the ICE recruits had failed to meet the standards for hire, including having disqualifying criminal backgrounds or lacking physical or academic requirements. The DHS told NBC News at the time that most of its new recruits are former law enforcement officers. Earlier this month, the agency said it would be retraining thousands of its officers who had received expedited training due to the hiring surge. The Oct. 10 incident involving Morales and Miguel Parra Hernandez was captured by several cameras. Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said the footage led investigators to believe that Morales deliberately ran over Parra to stop him during a chase. Parra is in rehabilitation, overseen by ICE officers, recovering from multiple injuries. If a similar incident occurred in a Harris County agency, Teare told NBC News on Monday, “every one of those people, whether or not they had gotten into any trouble or not, would be taken off the street and sent back through the full academy.” Morales was hired by ICE in August 2025 and had more training than other hires, his attorney, David Lindenmuth, said. He accused Teare of character assassination. “This Democratic district attorney has great issues with the conservative Republican Party government’s ICE agenda, and he’s trying to pick a fight with them, but he’s smashing this individual to do so,” Lindenmuth said. Lindenmuth said the car strike was accidental and happened as Morales reacted to avoid hitting a car that was in front of him. In response to criticism of Morales’ actions and to the training of ICE officers, an ICE spokesperson said in an email that “allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE.” “The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct,” the ICE spokesperson stated. Video of the collision captured by cameras from local businesses and bystanders recorded Morales pursuing Parra, who exits a stopped truck and begins running. Morales’ vehicle makes a quick left turn in front of a stopped vehicle and hits Parra. Morales’ body camera video captures the officer saying, “You got hit with the car, bro,” turning Parra over, straightening his leg, trying to pick him up from under his arms and telling others he should be moved into the car. Teare said Morales’ attempt to move Parra was “careless.” “These are not things that a law enforcement officer would ever do to someone that they had detained, with or without force, if they were complaining of injury,” Teare said. According to the DA’s office, Morales had two handcuffed arrestees sitting in the back of his car without seat belts when the vehicle hit Parra. To Teare, that was illustrative of the problems with the agency’s tactics and lack of proper training and vetting of ICE officers. Morales is the first ICE agent indicted in Texas. In May, prosecutors in Minnesota charged ICE enforcement officer Christian Castro in connection with the January shooting of Julio Sosa-Celis, and he was indicted on federal charges in September for making false statements to investigators about the case. Before joining ICE, Morales, originally from Brownsville, Texas, on the U.S.-Mexico border, worked several stints as a guard. One of those jobs was at the Port Isabel Detention Center, an ICE facility that has historically been the final stop before an immigrant is shuttled out of the country, Lindenmuth said. Morales started young, working from August 2012 to January 2013 as a corrections officer for Cameron County in Olmito, Texas, Lindenmuth said. He then joined the military and worked as a military police officer, though was not deployed during his two years of Army service, Lindenmuth said. An Army spokesperson said Morales left in 2014 with the rank of private first class. Morales then spent seven months with the Texas Department of Criminal Justice as a mid-level correctional officer overseeing the care and custody of inmates with limited supervision, according to Amanda Hernandez, a TDCJ spokeswoman. He resigned in 2018 while on probation with the agency for falsification of records, specifically documenting security rounds as completed when they had not been conducted, Hernandez said in an email. Lindenmuth said he did not immediately have further information about the probation. On Friday, Teare said he was “not familiar with a single agency that would have hired” Morales, after seeing his work record. Lindenmuth said his client is an ordained pastor of a Christian-based church. He said Morales studied to be a police chaplain at Universidad Cristiana Internacional El Shaddai in Dallas and has done missionary work in other countries. “He is a faith-based person,” Lindenmuth said. “You know, he is a good person who tries to help people.”

articles.title: US will mediate upcoming Ukraine-Russia talks in Abu Dhabi, Witkoff says
articles.summary: U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff announced U.S.-mediated peace talks between Ukraine and Russia on Nov. 10 and 11, focusing on security arrangements and de-escalation.
articles.body: U.S. officials will mediate a new round of talks between Ukraine and Russia next week with the goal of delivering "lasting security for generations to come," U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff said on Monday. Witkoff said the U.S.-mediated negotiations will be held on Nov. 10 and 11 in Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates. "The United States will mediate working-level negotiations between Ukraine and Russia on November 10–11 in Abu Dhabi, advancing President Trump’s mission to end the war. Discussions will focus on post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace," Witkoff wrote on X. INSIDE MELANIA TRUMP'S SECRET DIPLOMATIC ROLE IN THE RUSSIA-UKRAINE CEASEFIRE DEAL Ahead of next week's peace talks, U.S. negotiators will meet this week in Brussels with representatives from France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the EU and NATO. "Additionally, American negotiators will meet this week in Brussels with representatives from France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the EU, and NATO to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine, Europe’s post-war security architecture, and economic opportunities to support Ukraine’s reconstruction," Witkoff said. The push by the U.S. government builds upon earlier diplomatic discussions held in Kyiv, Oslo and St. Petersburg, as the Trump administration continues efforts to broker an end to the war following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. "We look forward to building on the progress made in Kyiv, Oslo, and St. Petersburg toward a comprehensive, durable peace agreement that delivers lasting security for generations to come," Witkoff said. articles.title: Ebola outbreak kills more than 5,300 people in DR Congo
articles.summary: The Bundibugyo strain has spread to Kenya and Uganda, while two in Nigeria returned negative results.
articles.body:
The death toll from the latest Ebola outbreak in Africa has surpassed 5,300, with the majority of cases recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), according to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).

The DRC is the epicentre of the latest outbreak, having declared its 17th – and largest – Ebola outbreak in mid-May.

According to data from the Africa CDC on Monday, the outbreak has killed 5,376 people: 5,372 in the DRC and two each in Kenya and Uganda.

The Bundibugyo strain of the virus, responsible for the current outbreak, has infected some 10,444 people in the DRC, Uganda and Kenya, with a death rate of more than 50 percent.

The virus has crossed borders several times in recent months.

Neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 cases, almost all involving people who had travelled from the DRC, before being declared Ebola-free in August.

Kenya recorded two deaths and nine infections in October, marking the first recorded cases of Ebola in the country.

In Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, health authorities said two rounds of testing of two suspected cases in the northeast region confirmed the samples were negative.

Abuja reported its first imported case in October, the first in more than a decade. It has no recorded deaths.

In France, a single case involving a health worker returning from the DRC was reported in July.

There are no approved treatments or vaccines to combat the rare Bundibugyo strain.

In recent weeks, clinical trials have begun with the Ervebo vaccine, which has proved effective against the more common Zaire strain.

articles.title: North Korea denies being behind $6.3bn Binance crypto hack
articles.summary: US government agencies and cyber analysts have blamed Pyongyang for the record-breaking heist.
articles.body:
North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance , calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric".

Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un , said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image.

The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history.

This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy.

Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor.

The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group.

"The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement.

"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said.

Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack

Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far

But Pyongyang has been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks in recent years - accusations that it has denied.

The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.

Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said.

The country has consistently denied such claims.

Kim Yo Jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace".

Kim Yo-jong: North Korea's heir apparent?

The BBC has contacted Binance for comment. Since the hack, the crypto giant has largely focused its public statements on the technical nature of the breach and its response to protect users.

The company said last week that initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals.

Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack.

A net $5.27bn has been withdrawn from the exchange since transactions resumed on Sunday, according to data posted on Tuesday by Binance. It also said the level of transactions has now stabilised.

The company has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack and that it has so far covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach.

articles.title: U.S. military carries out limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island, U.S. officials say
articles.summary: The strikes, which appeared to be limited as opposed to a full return to hostilities, came on the eve of crucial American midterm elections.
articles.body: The U.S. military carried out limited strikes Monday on Iran’s Qeshm Island, according to two U.S. officials. The officials said the U.S. attacks, which came on the eve of crucial U.S. midterm elections and as the Middle East is anxious about the possibility of a return to all-out war, were not a resumption of major combat operations in Iran. They described the attacks as self-defense in response to Iran’s ongoing efforts to target maritime shipping and U.S. assets. The U.S. continues to intercept drones and missiles that are targeting shipping every day, one of the U.S. officials said. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has routinely targeted and shot at U.S. manned and unmanned aircraft over the Strait of Hormuz and in the area over the past few weeks, one of the U.S. officials said. The U.S. is occasionally striking Iranian missile launchers in self-defense when the Revolutionary Guard shoots at U.S. aircraft, the official said. Iran tried to target a U.S. aircraft again, leading to the U.S. strike on Qeshm to take out the launcher, the official said, calling it part of ongoing operations. A third U.S. official said, “This was a defensive measure for Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against U.S. assets.” Iranian state media reported that five explosions were heard Monday on Qeshm Island. President Donald Trump had said the U.S. would not launch strikes on Iran before Tuesday’s midterm elections. The unpopular Iran war and the resulting impact on U.S. gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for Republicans as they try to keep control of Congress. The administration was last known to have carried out some attacks in early September, but thousands of U.S. troops remain in the waters off Iran to maintain a naval blockade aimed at preventing tankers carrying Iranian oil from getting to the global market. A third aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are also on their way to the Middle East. Earlier Monday, Vice President JD Vance offered measured optimism that a deal can still be struck to prevent Trump from following through on his threat to potentially order new strikes on Iran after the midterm elections. Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, last week, few details of which have been offered by the White House. Trump told reporters the letter was focused on assisting Iran with “medical supplies and various things.” Vance suggested Monday that there was reason to believe the U.S. and Iran could still come to an agreement. “We’ve had a number of good conversations with the Iranians,” he told reporters when he was asked about the letter, adding that he and Trump “both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement. We’re going to keep on working at it.” The region remains on edge about the prospect of the U.S.’ resuming full-scale operations against Iran. The back-channel efforts are playing out as Israel and some Middle East allies lobby Trump on the way forward in the eight-month-old war, which has rattled global markets and wreaked havoc on Iran. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had pushed for renewed strikes even before the Israeli election last week as he sought to highlight his security credentials to a public deeply scarred by Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack. But the war has also loomed large for American voters ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections. Oil prices dropped sharply Monday as renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war appeared to show signs of progress. Trump noted the drop Monday in a speech in Washington, which was billed as his closing argument to Americans, and sought to minimize the scale of the conflict, which has cost U.S. taxpayers at least $47 billion. “I don’t know if you even call it a war, because we haven’t been doing any fighting for months,” Trump said. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has repeatedly said Iran is open to diplomatic talks. “While our Brave Armed Forces are fully prepared to defend the Homeland, Iran continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed,” he wrote on X last week.

articles.title: Christmas 2026 stamps unveiled by Royal Mail
articles.summary: The annual Christmas collection of five stamps feature scenes from the Nativity.
articles.body:
Royal Mail has unveiled its Christmas stamps for this year - featuring scenes from the Nativity.

The series of five stamps have been jointly created by graphic designer Gareth Howat and illustrator Rebecca Sutherland.

The stamps depict familiar scenes of Mary and Joseph travelling, baby Jesus, an angel, the shepherds and the Three Wise Men.

This year's collection marks the 60th anniversary of the first-ever Christmas special stamp.

Sutherland said it was an "absolute honour" to be given the opportunity to illustrate the Christmas stamps for the Royal Mail.

She said she has loved stamps since she was a child and had even collected them. "Being asked to create a set myself feels incredibly special," she added.

The Christmas stamps from recent years have featured snowy scenes of UK cathedrals, or lyrics from famous carols - although 2025 also showed scenes from the Nativity.

The first Christmas stamp collection came out in December 1966 after a children's art competition was announced by the then-postmaster Tony Benn.

David Gold, of Royal Mail, said: "We hope this year's Christmas stamps will add an extra touch of festive magic to the millions of greetings sent to family and friends at home and around the world."

articles.title: US urges Venezuela to follow phased plan for democratic transition
articles.summary: This comes as leading opposition leader returns to Venezuela and hints at criticism of Trump administration.
articles.body:
The United States has urged Venezuela to continue on a phased plan of economic recovery and political reconciliation before embarking on democratic elections.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio discussed the gradual plan during a meeting on the country’s political future with Venezuelan Minister of Foreign Affairs Oliver Blanco on Monday. The meeting comes nearly a year after US forces abducted former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro from Caracas and brought him to the US to face drug trafficking and other charges.

Neither Rubio nor Blanco spoke to the media after the meeting, but in a readout. The State Department said in a readout that Washington had reaffirmed President Donald Trump’s “three-phase plan for Venezuela: stabilization, economic recovery and political reconciliation, and democratic transition”.

Last week, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returned to her country, thanking the US president and Rubio for their support. Machado, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate who gifted her medal to Trump in 2025, said she had come to organise a movement in preparation for Venezuelan elections.

Rubio “has set out a sequence of events aimed at moving toward a democratic transition that makes clear the holding of presidential elections in 2027”, she said.

Machado is balancing an election campaign with a Trump administration that has sought to extract oil from Venezuela by striking deals with the government of interim President Delcy Rodriguez, who served as Maduro’s vice president and took over after his abduction.

In September, the Trump administration said it had struck a deal with Venezuela that would give Washington a stake in about one-fifth of the country’s oil resources.

The US said it was creating a joint venture with North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), owned by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, which is the second-largest private oil operator in Venezuela, behind Chevron.

Under the deal, Caracas is giving the company 100-year rights over 17 oilfields with proven reserves of 65 billion barrels. The Pentagon will have a 35 percent stake in NABEP, and the US will be guaranteed the right to buy 20 percent of its oil output at cost, the Trump administration has said.

Shortly before Machado’s statements on Thursday, Rodriguez assured the nation that elections would be held in Venezuela “with the world as witness”, but did not specify a date.

When asked about a possible meeting with Rodriguez, Machado said she had not received any message from the interim president or from Washington.

In remarks after returning Venezuela, Machado seemed sceptical of the oil agreement with the US.

“This agreement does not reflect the levels of transparency that Venezuelan society wants,” Machado said.

articles.title: Delhi AQI turns 'hazardous' at 451 ahead of Diwali; GRAP-II curbs enforced across NCR
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi's air quality continued to deteriorate ahead of Diwali, with the national capital's overall Air Quality Index (AQI) touching 451 at 8 am
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi's air quality continued to deteriorate ahead of Diwali, with the national capital's overall Air Quality Index (AQI) touching 451 at 8 am on Tuesday, placing it in the "hazardous" category and highlighting the worsening pollution situation across the city.Data from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) showed that several monitoring stations reported AQI levels in the severe category, while a number of other locations recorded very poor air quality.Among the worst-affected areas, Rohini recorded an AQI of 429, followed by Punjabi Bagh at 424 and Bawana at 408, with all three locations falling in the severe category.Several other parts of the city continued to breathe very poor air. Patparganj recorded an AQI of 379, followed by R K Puram at 374, ITO at 373, Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium at 355, Okhla Phase-2 and Chandni Chowk at 352 each, while Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) recorded 328.Meanwhile, relatively lower pollution levels were reported at a few monitoring stations, although air quality remained in the poor category. Indira Gandhi International (IGI) Airport's Terminal 3 recorded an AQI of 287, followed by Anand Vihar at 279, Uttam Nagar at 274 and IMD Lodhi Road at 226.Amid the worsening air quality, Delhi Police conducted a checking drive at the Ghazipur border as restrictions on vehicle entry came into force under Stage-II of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP).The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) invoked Stage-II of GRAP across the entire National Capital Region (NCR) on Monday in view of the rising pollution levels. The restrictions came into immediate effect, adding to the measures already in place under Stage-I.Under the enhanced curbs, municipal corporations, traffic police and pollution control boards across Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan have been directed to step up enforcement measures.As part of the action plan, daily mechanical or vacuum sweeping will be undertaken, along with water sprinkling mixed with dust suppressants, on heavy-traffic corridors and congestion points. Authorities have been asked to prioritise these activities before peak traffic hours.In addition, inspections and remedial measures will be intensified at identified pollution hotspots and Construction and Demolition (C&D) sites across the NCR.(With agency inputs).You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Trump calls Iran conflict a 'soft war,' insists US holds the cards ahead of midterm elections
articles.summary: Trump called the Iran conflict a "soft war" on "Hannity" just hours after the United States struck Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.

"We're not fighting a war … When was the last time we fired anything? This isn't a war, this is a very soft war," Trump said Monday on "Hannity." Iran could be a key deciding issue as voters go to the polls on Election Day Tuesday as Americans continue to grapple with surging gas prices and the economic fallout from the United States’ conflict, which began eight months ago. When was the last time you saw us fighting with them? We go months and months, we talk," Trump told host Sean Hannity. "This is not much of a war, Sean, because there hasn't been shooting for months." TRUMP ADMIN THREATENS IRAN WITH 'CONSEQUENCES' AS ALLIES CONVENE AMID THREATS OF POST-ELECTION ESCALATION Trump’s comments come shortly after the United States struck Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz Monday after Iran fired at a U.S. aircraft. The president said Monday that he was in no hurry to resume military strikes against Iran but warned that the U.S. will give Iran "the hammer" soon if the latest round of peace talks are not fruitful. articles.title: 'Lousy con artist': BJP attacks Rahul Gandhi after his 'foreign help' jibe at PM Modi
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Tuesday hit back at Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi after he accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Tuesday hit back at Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi after he accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi of becoming PM and remaining in office with the help of foreign forces. BJP spokesperson C R Kesavan questioned Rahul's foreign visits and alleged that the Congress leader had sought foreign interference in India's internal affairs.In a post on X, Kesavan called Rahul a "lousy con artist" and accused him of making misleading claims that backfire. articles.title: Bangladesh: Wage protests force hundreds of garment factories to close
articles.summary: These factories, which manufacture for brands like H&M and Uniqlo, rely on millions of lowly paid workers.
articles.body:
Hundreds of garment factories in Bangladesh have been forced to closed after days-long protests by workers demanding higher wages.

On Sunday, protests in the capital Dhaka turned violent with protesters blocking roads, vandalising factories and setting vehicles on fire. They also clashed with police, who fired tear gas to disperse them. Police later said that dozens of protesters had been arrested.

Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($242; £180), more than double the current standard, citing rising costs of living.

Bangladesh's textile industry employs around four million workers and manufactures garments for major global brands including H&M, Primark and Uniqlo.

There are fears in the industry that the prolonged unrest could disrupt production and affect international buyers, state news agency BSS reported.

The garment industry generates nearly $40bn every year for Bangladesh, accounting for around 10% of its GDP.

The South Asian nation is the world's second-largest garment exporter after China - but its workers are among the lowest-paid in the world, taking home around 13,000 taka ($105; £78) a month.

"We want the government to accept our demands and increase our wages. [And] they need to instruct landlords and homeowners not to raise rent and ensure that the prices of essential commodities remain affordable," one female worker told BBC Bangla.

"Food prices, cooking gas and electricity bills have all gone up," Mamun, a 28-year-old factory worker, told AFP. "The government must either bring down the prices of essential commodities or raise our wages."

The government announced on Sunday that it had established a board to review workers' wages, and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman held an emergency meeting with ministers to address the unrest.

But demonstrations continued on Monday in Dhaka and nearby manufacturing hubs including Ashulia, Gazipur and Narayanganj.

Around 670 factories suspended operations on Monday, according to reports by Reuters and AFP, and hundreds in these areas will remain shut on Tuesday.

At least 29 protesters were arrested as of Monday, according to Dhaka police Deputy Commissioner Mohidul Islam, who said that those who created an "unstable environment in the garment factories" would come under the law.

Authorities have accused the Awami League, the banned political party of former leader Sheikh Hasina, for taking advantage of the protest movement to instigate violence - though they did not provide any evidence of this.

Home minister Salahuddin Ahmed threatened punitive action against protesters who were trying to "destabilise the country" "under the guise of labour protests".

Babul Akhter, a workers' representative on the wage board, urged protesters to go back to work on Monday, promising to "fight for [their] fair wages".

"I tell my fellow workers, return to work. Don't give in to anyone's incitement."

articles.title: North Korea denies involvement in Binance hack and criticizes FBI probe as ‘a trite provocation’
articles.summary: The FBI had accused North Korean hackers of stealing more than $6 billion from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange.
articles.body: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korea on Tuesday denied its involvement in the recent cryptocurrency heist at Binance, dismissing as “a trite provocation” a U.S. announcement that North Korean hackers were behind the incident. Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record. The FBI later said the theft was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, attributing the attack to a hacking group known as TraderTraitor, which was also behind a $1.5 billion hack of the Bybit exchange last year. On Tuesday, Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, called the FBI announcement “a trite provocation” and “an absurd rhetoric.” “This is not the first time that the U.S. has attempted to spread misunderstanding of the DPRK in the international community, blindly linking the DPRK with the ‘cyber crime’ incidents whenever they occur on an international scale,” she said in a statement, using the abbreviation of North Korea’s official name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. “On this occasion, we confirmed Washington’s hostile attitude toward the DPRK once again and are closely monitoring a variety of persistent provocations of the U.S. against our state,” Kim Yo Jong said. Outside experts say North Korea has increasingly turned to cryptocurrency theft and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency, helping sustain its struggling economy and fund its nuclear program in the face of stringent U.S.-led international sanctions and other challenges. In December 2022, South Korea’s spy agency estimated that North Korean hackers had stolen 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets over the previous five years. Although the country has mostly denied involvement, North Korea has been linked to numerous major cyberattacks in past years, including a 2013 campaign that paralyzed the servers of South Korean financial institutions, the 2014 hacking of Sony Pictures and the WannaCry malware attack of 2017. South Korea’s Foreign Ministry said Monday that North Korea’s illicit cyber activities pose an increasing threat to the global digital economy and that Seoul was closely cooperating with the United States and the broader international community to address the threat. The Binance heist came as North Korea has ramped up its weapons tests in a likely bid to increase its leverage in potential diplomacy with the U.S. after President Donald Trump expressed his desire to restore diplomacy with Kim Jong Un. On Tuesday, North Korea said it had tested a new cluster warhead for strategic cruise missiles. Asked by reporters later during a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, Trump suggested investigators were not yet certain that North Korea was involved. “I’m not concerned. We’re learning about it,” Trump said of the case. “We don’t know if it’s North Korea,” he added, though saying investigators could still determine that it was. In her Tuesday statement, Kim Yo Jong said: “We have issues to reconsider in diverse aspects as regards the very unpleasant U.S. hostile attitude.”

articles.title: Michael Blackson opened a tuition-free school in his father's Ghanaian hometown; a new community basketball court was added to its campus in 2026
articles.summary: Michael Blackson Academy, a tuition-free school in Nsaba in Ghana’s Central Region, now has a community basketball court on its campus.
articles.body: Michael Blackson Academy, a tuition-free school in Nsaba in Ghana’s Central Region, now has a community basketball court on its campus. Giants of Africa, the non-profit organisation founded by sports executive Masai Ujiri, unveiled the facility on 10 March 2026 in partnership with actor and comedian Michael Blackson, who started the school in 2023. The state-of-the-art court gives pupils a modern place to play, train and learn teamwork alongside their lessons. It also shows how a celebrity’s personal investment in his community, a charitable partnership and free schooling can come together to widen opportunity for underserved young people across Ghana.Why a free school in Ghana tackles overcrowded public schools and opens doors for underserved youthThe academy was set up to help address overcrowding in public schools, The Guardian Nigeria reported, while expanding access to education and leadership development. The Michael Blackson Foundation describes it as a free-for-all school for children from underprivileged backgrounds, with classrooms, gyms and computer labs in a safe, modern setting. Sport and music activities run alongside lessons so pupils can develop their talents and interests, and the foundation says the school is committed to breaking the cycle of poverty through education.Blackson has described the school as the fulfilment of something he always wanted to do. At its grand opening, he said it was the greatest day of his life and that foundational education “shouldn’t come with financial barriers”.How Giants of Africa’s Built Within initiative is putting basketball courts across the continentThe Guardian Nigeria reports that the Nsaba court is the 46th built by Giants of Africa and its third in Ghana. It forms part of the Built Within initiative, which aims to create 100 community basketball courts across Africa.Ujiri said in a statement that it was “powerful to see how Michael has invested back into his community”. He described the academy as a place where young people in Ghana can learn, grow and believe in themselves, and said the court will make their education richer. He added that the organisation’s court builds are meant to teach sportsmanship and cooperation while letting children enjoy the game.How donations to the Michael Blackson Foundation open up quality education for children in needThe foundation’s appeal rests on a simple promise that a single gift can change the course of a child’s life. It asks supporters to help children gain access to quality education and reach their full potential, and says donations will allow it to give young people the chance to become leaders in their communities. The foundation also ties giving to the wider goals of building sustainable communities and creating brighter futures.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
