articles.title: El-Sayed, Rogers hold dueling rallies as bitter campaign comes to a close
articles.summary: The events come as Haley Stevens opined on why she withdrew support for the US Senate Democratic nominee.
articles.body:
On the eve of the consequential midterm elections in the United States, candidates in Michigan’s bitter, hard-fought US Senate race have made their final appeals to voters in a contest that could help determine control of Congress.

During duelling campaign rallies on Monday evening, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers offered contrasting visions to the state’s voters. Despite dramatic, late-breaking developments, polls suggest the tenuous race has slipped further out of reach for the Republican Party.

As Tom Petty’s I Won’t Back Down played in the background, Rogers took the stage in Rochester Hills, Michigan, to talk about the race he described as a battle for the “heart and soul of the country”.

“Are you guys ready to fight for freedom tomorrow?” the former congressman asked the crowd. “Are you ready to send a message to the rest of the country that we are the ones that defeated the Democrat Socialists of America?”

Half an hour away in Detroit, at a rally with members of the United Auto Workers labour group, El-Sayed focused on his cost-of-living platform. He touched on the barrage of dark themes that have reverberated across the state – and the nation – in the closing days of the campaign, including a litany of anti-Muslim rhetoric.

“You might think that in a moment when gas is too expensive and people can’t afford their groceries, that if you wanted to win an election, you might want to talk about gas and groceries,” El-Sayed told rally attendees. “They don’t wanna talk about gas and groceries. They wanna talk about me and my name and my faith.”

The primary instigator of those attacks, US President Donald Trump, has said that El-Sayed, whose family emigrated from Egypt, would “invite hordes of jihadis” to the US. Trump has also frequently purposefully misnamed the Democrat, calling him “Abdul Ramadan”, or emphasising his middle name, “Mohammed”.

“I don’t even care if [Trump] knows what my name is,” El-Sayed said. “Because after tomorrow, we’re gonna make sure he calls me senator.”

But a shocking endorsement of El-Sayed’s opponent from a fellow Democrat may prove pivotal, as late-deciding Michiganders prepare to enter the voting booth on Tuesday.

Representative Haley Stevens, a Democrat who lost to El-Sayed in the race for the US Senate nomination during the state’s primary earlier this year, sent shockwaves across the country on Sunday when she broke ranks and threw her support behind Rogers.

Stevens, who had struggled in a series of interviews to explain why she decided to back the Republican in the race, posted a lengthy message to social media Monday detailing what went into her decision. She said it was based on an advertisement unaffiliated with El-Sayed’s campaign that tied US support for Israel to rising grocery costs, as well as being “shut out” of the campaign.

“Mike Rogers and I disagree on many things. But Michigan has to elect a senator and there is no neutral choice that absolves me of responsibility,” Stevens wrote on X. “Once I concluded that Abdul El-Sayed is not fit to serve in the United States Senate, I had to confront who should.”

Stevens, who chided her fellow Democrats for their reaction to her endorsement, hinted at possible future political plans when she leaves office in January. “We can build a stronger, more welcoming, more courageous Democratic Party,” she said. “And I plan to help lead that effort”.

Attendees at Rogers’s rally applauded when he highlighted Stevens’s and other Democratic endorsements he had received.

“That is a special kind of courage,” he said of Stevens.

The crowd then burst into chants of “Haley!”

A New York Times-Siena poll released on Sunday suggested El-Sayed is leading Rogers by 11 percentage points – 53 to 42 percent – among likely voters. The poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points.

articles.title: Israeli forces release Al Jazeera journalist in occupied West Bank
articles.summary: Video of the arrest shows Israeli forces leading Montaser Nassar, who was blindfolded and handcuffed, into a vehicle.
articles.body:
Israeli forces have released Al Jazeera correspondent Montaser Nassar and several other people hours after arresting them during a raid in the southern occupied West Bank.

Nassar was arrested early on Tuesday at his home in Dura, near the city of Hebron.

Video of the arrest shows Israeli forces leading Nassar, who was blindfolded and handcuffed, into a military vehicle.

Reporting from Hebron, Al Jazeera’s Mohamed al-Atrash said at least 20 Palestinians were detained in the raid on Dura, including Nassar, before Israeli forces withdrew from the town hours later.

Nassar had been reporting on the raid near his home when troops moved on his house.

“He went towards the door, according to his wife’s account, but saw soldiers advancing towards the residential building where he lives before the army raided this particular house,” Atrash said.

“The army entered and assaulted his wife before confiscating our colleague Montaser’s personal phone.” Nassar was then taken away with other detainees at about 2:30am (00:30 GMT).

Atrash said such raids are “part of the daily reality experienced in the West Bank”. Detainees are either jailed or released after field interrogations by officers from Israel’s Shin Bet security service.

Israel is holding at least 40 Palestinian journalists, “half of whom are held under administrative detention without charge”, Atrash added.

The arrest comes amid mounting pressure on Palestinian journalists in the occupied West Bank. The Palestinian Journalists Syndicate recorded 84 alleged press violations by Israeli forces and settlers in August alone, including arrests and a death in custody.

Last week, Israeli forces raided Al-Ghad TV’s Hebron office. Israel raided and shut down Al Jazeera’s Ramallah bureau in the West Bank in 2024.

articles.title: UK to double wait for permanent residency, with exemptions for care workers
articles.summary: Under new rules, most workers will have to wait 10 years to settle in the UK, but higher earners can qualify sooner.
articles.body:
The United Kingdom has revised its immigration rules, doubling the time most foreign workers must wait to qualify for permanent residency to 10 years and making refugees who arrive on “small boats” wait as long as 30 years.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, speaking in Parliament on Monday, said hundreds of thousands of care workers will be exempt from the hardline rules, offering a concession amid a political outcry within the governing Labour Party.

Permanent residency, known in the UK as indefinite leave to remain, carries the right to work, study, use the free National Health Service and claim welfare benefits. Until now, it has been granted after five years.

The new rules, set to take effect next year, tie eligibility for permanent residency to income.

People who earn more than 50,000 pounds a year ($67,000) will still be able to apply after five years, and those earning more than 125,000 pounds ($167,500) after three. Everyone else will be placed on the 10-year path. The median salary in the UK is about 39,000 pounds (roughly $52,000).

The rules will apply retroactively to workers already in the country.

“Settlement should not be automatic. It should be earned,” Mahmood, the home secretary, told Parliament, adding that the changes would restore fairness by linking the right to settle to what immigrants contribute.

“Those who contribute most will settle fastest,” she said. “Those who don’t play by the rules will be refused or wait longer.”

The UK government first proposed last year that lower-skilled workers wait 10 to 15 years for permanent residency.

But the plan drew fierce opposition from unions and parts of the Labour Party, particularly over its effect on care workers, who are often poorly paid and work in a sector that has long struggled to fill vacancies. Many of them arrived in the early 2020s, as the country was reeling from the COVID-19 pandemic, to fill gaps left by European workers who had departed after Brexit.

Under the revised plan, care workers will be able to settle after five years if they have met the conditions of their visas and earn at least 25,000 pounds ($33,500) a year.

Mahmood said the rules would offer a path for care workers “who worked hard and answered our call when we needed them”.

As for refugees, those who arrive through one of the government’s “new safe and legal routes” will be able to settle after five years, she said. For other refugees, the standard wait will become 20 years, reduced to 10 years for those who work or study. Anyone who arrived by an “illegal method”, such as by small boat, could wait up to 30 years for settlement, she said.

Under the new rules, applicants will also be disqualified if they have a criminal record, cannot speak English “to a high standard”, owe money to the government, or have not made at least three years of national insurance contributions.

Mahmood said the overhaul would mean that half a million people would settle later than they otherwise would have, saving the government billions of pounds in benefits.

In total, the government estimates that as many as 1.4 million people will receive settled status between 2026 and 2030.

The changes, announced after a 12-week public consultation that drew more than 200,000 responses, are part of a broader effort to tighten immigration rules after arrivals surged following Brexit.

They are a response to political pressure, including from Nigel Farage’s populist Reform UK party, which has surged in popularity in recent years with calls for stricter migration controls. Reform UK has sought to depict the arrivals of refugees on small boats across the English Channel as a crisis, and anti-immigration activists have staged protests, including outside facilities that house asylum seekers.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government has said that increased law enforcement cooperation between the UK and France has helped reduce the number of people making the crossing so far this year by more than 40 percent compared with 2025.

articles.title: Reddit blasts Australia’s ‘inept’ social media ban as court challenge begins
articles.summary: Reddit and a libertarian advocacy group are contesting the 2025 Australian law, which bans large social media platforms from letting people under age 16 have accounts.
articles.body: CANBERRA, Australia — Australia’s world-first teen social media ban was “ill thought out” and amounted to a “profound restriction on political debate,” a lawyer for messaging platform Reddit told the country’s top court in the first legal challenge to the law. Reddit and a libertarian advocacy group have taken to the High Court to contest the Australian law, which bans large social media platforms from letting people under the age of 16 have accounts and took effect in late 2025 amid support from parents and opposition from the tech firms. A successful challenge could usher in more opposition from affected companies and slow a global uptake of similar policies as lawmakers from Britain to Malaysia roll out the measures in an effort to protect youth mental and physical health. The Australian government and its communications minister, a named defendant, have said they will defend the law. Addressing the court, Perry Herzfeld, for Reddit, said barring people under 16 from holding social media accounts stopped them from creating or responding to content on what he called the most important means of communication in the modern world. “That is a very profound restriction on political debate in Australia,” Herzfeld said. “There is a very substantial restriction on what young people can now do.” Reddit agreed with the Australians’ harm-minimization aim but the law failed to do so, Herzfeld said, terming the legislation “ill thought out” and “inept” since it did not call for any specific measure to keep out minors and failed to restrict other online services where cyberbullying takes place, such as gaming websites. While social media content can typically only be created or commented on by logged-in account holders, vast amounts of material are visible to people with no accounts, he said. “If the Commonwealth is worried about particular features (of social media), it should regulate the features, which it has not done,” he said. Since the ban went live, multiple studies, including by Australian regulator the eSafety Commissioner, have found that most of the country’s teenagers under the cutoff age continue to use social media. The government has since doubled the maximum fine for non-compliance to 99 million Australian dollars ($69.5 million), given the eSafety Commissioner greater discovery powers, and said it is preparing an enforcement lawsuit against some of the biggest platforms.

articles.title: Israeli forces kill four in Gaza as fifth Palestinian dies of wounds
articles.summary: Nearly 1,600 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since a US-brokered ‘ceasefire’ took effect in October last year.
articles.body:
Israeli forces have killed at least four Palestinians in attacks across Gaza, while a fifth person died of wounds sustained in an earlier assault, according to medical sources and media reports.

At least two people were killed in a gun attack and an air raid on southern Khan Younis on Monday, while a third was killed in a drone attack on the central al-Musaddar village, medical sources said.

The fourth person died in a strike on a vehicle in northern Gaza City’s Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood, according to the Wafa news agency. It identified the victim as Hani Hamed Kahil and said five others were wounded in the attack.

The Israeli military said it targeted Palestinian fighters in three strikes, but provided no further details.

Wafa reported that a fifth person, Youssef Abu Younis, also died of injuries sustained in an Israeli attack on a police post in al-Mawasi on Sunday. His death brought the number of deaths reported on Monday to five.

Earlier, at least five Palestinian police officers were killed in an attack on Sunday.

Elsewhere in Gaza City, three Palestinians were wounded on Monday when a minibus belonging to a community kitchen was hit in Zeitoun.

According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, Israeli attacks have killed at least 1,593 Palestinians since the United States-brokered “ceasefire” began in October 2025, and wounded 5,748 others. Overall, Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed at least 74,609 Palestinians and wounded 175,872 people.

The latest attacks came amid efforts to secure shelter for displaced Palestinians before winter.

Israeli Army Radio reported that Nickolay Mladenov , the high representative of the Board of Peace, established by the US to oversee a so-called peace plan in Gaza, arrived in Israel on Monday to seek permission to bring in tents and push for steps to accelerate reconstruction.

The scale of the need in Gaza remains vast. The United Nations migration agency said on October 9 that nearly two million people required shelter assistance and half of Gaza’s tents and makeshift shelters needed replacing, leaving families exposed as winter approached.

articles.title: California’s Bay Area debates data centres ahead of US midterm elections
articles.summary: At least seven Bay Area cities have passed data centre moratoriums, despite the region’s reputation as an AI hub.
articles.body:
Oakland, California – Protesters dressed as cardboard robots chanted and danced to a drumbeat as they protested against new data centres outside Oakland City Hall last month.

Their concerns largely focused on how the centres — which process large amounts of digital information — might strain the energy grid.

The result, they argued, would not only be environmental harm but also sky-high electricity bills for local households.

“Power prices have gone up so much in Oakland that some people are thinking of shutting off their power,” said Carlos Gutierrez, an activist for Communities for a Better Environment, an environmental justice group.

“And the city is planning to provide power to a data centre instead.”

Opposition to data centres is growing across the United States, as residents express concern about their rapid expansion.

More than 3,000 data centres already operate in the country, with more than 1,500 others in development, according to the Pew Research Center.

But the backlash is perhaps most striking in California’s San Francisco Bay Area, a region considered to be the heart of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom.

Major AI companies such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta are based in the Bay Area, and the industry’s growth has been credited with fuelling a local economic renaissance.

Data centres house the advanced computer chips and servers needed to run AI-powered services such as Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s ChatGPT.

But they also require 24-hour power and a large supply of water to cool their processors.

Even with such cooling technology, data centres are notorious for emitting heat, leading to an increase in land surface temperatures as high as 9 degrees Celsius (16 degrees Fahrenheit).

Concerns about the cost of rapid data centre growth, both environmentally and financially, have catapulted the issue into the discourse around Tuesday’s midterm elections.

In the final two months before the vote, at least seven Bay Area cities, including San Francisco and Richmond, have passed temporary moratoriums on data centre construction.

They include Oakland, which passed a data centre moratorium on October 6, after days of protest.

Local politicians competing in Tuesday’s midterms have also used the topic as a wedge issue, to rally support among certain pockets of voters.

One of the most closely watched races in the Bay Area is for the seat left vacant by longtime Democratic leader Nancy Pelosi. After 39 years in the House of Representatives, Pelosi is retiring at the end of the year.

Two Democrats are competing in Tuesday’s election to fill her position in Congress: San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan and state Senator Scott Wiener.

Each one has staked out a different position on AI data centres. Wiener, for instance, opposes any ban on data centres.

“A blanket data centre moratorium could undermine AI regulation,” he told the publication Mission Local.

Chan, meanwhile, has pledged to seek a nationwide moratorium on data centres, at least until responsible AI regulation is put in place.

“Let’s start with a moratorium on data centres. Allow us to have that moment to regulate artificial intelligence,” she said at a debate in October.

Chan played a leading role in passing San Francisco’s moratorium in early October.

A poll from the University of Southern California showed Wiener leading Chan 47 percent to 41, as of mid-October.

“Right now, data centre opposition is an issue that unifies the US public like no other,” said Shum Preston, a political analyst based in San Francisco.

So far, there has been relatively little opposition to the data centre moratoriums in local hearings. But he speculates that there may be several reasons for the lack of pushback to the bans.

Among them are the surveys indicating widespread public backlash to data centre creation.

An October CNBC poll found that 63 percent of registered US voters oppose building data centres within 16 kilometres, or 10 miles, of their homes.

“Data centres poll very poorly, and developers probably don’t want to put their supervisor friends in trouble ahead of elections. So they probably let this pass,” Preston said.

He also signalled that the short-term nature of the moratoriums may be a factor.

Certain Bay Area cities like San Francisco, Brisbane and Oakland paused construction on data centres for 45 days, with the option to extend the ban later.

Opponents of the moratoriums “will be more vocal when” the 45 days end, Preston said. By that time, the heat of the midterm election season will also have settled, he added.

“That’s when the hearings will get more contentious,” he said.

Another hurdle facing the moratoriums is the lack of transparency surrounding data centre construction.

Supervisor Shamann Walton, who sponsored San Francisco’s moratorium ordinance, has argued that the city’s definition of “data centres” is outdated.

Created in 2001 — long before the AI boom — the city planning code defines data centres as “internet service exchanges”, a definition that may not accurately characterise the technology today.

Walton said the outdated language has made it hard for authorities to count how many data centres exist in the city.

Not being able to identify data centres can also prevent city officials from monitoring their power and water usage.

“We cannot use 2001 rules to regulate 2026 technology,” he said in a September 14 statement.

Another issue is the time it takes to carry out the necessary environmental assessments. The moratoriums may not offer enough time for a comprehensive review.

“Forty-five days is hardly enough time to document and study the impacts and then frame regulations,” said Roger Lin, senior attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity, a US environmental nonprofit.

He added that legal barriers limit access to such information from the data centres themselves.

“Data centres often have nondisclosure agreements, so even local air quality boards may not know the impact of data centres on air quality,” said Lin.

Still, AI industry supporters have touted the growth of the data centres as evidence of a flourishing industry, with positive downstream effects for US communities.

Anthropic, for instance, is preparing an initial public offering (IPO) that is likely to raise billions of dollars.

But critics warn that the company’s growth may not translate into an economic boom for the San Francisco Bay Area overall.

Instead, residents fear unequal economic growth that primarily benefits the wealthy. Already, San Francisco faces some of the highest and fastest-growing home rental prices in the country.

At a hearing at San Francisco City Hall, a resident vented their frustrations about the data centres to the supervisors.

“This city is less for humans and more for robots and billionaires,” the resident said.

articles.title: ‘Going hungry’: Garment workers in Bangladesh say wages barely cover needs
articles.summary: Tens of thousands of workers in world’s second-largest apparel exporter hit the streets to demand better minimum wages.
articles.body:
Dhaka, Bangladesh – Laili Begum can no longer afford to keep her two children in school. There are days when the 37-year-old garment worker struggles to put even one proper meal on the table.

An experienced sewing operator at Virtual Bottoms Limited, a ready-made garments factory near Bangladesh’s capital Dhaka, Begum earns around 15,000 taka ($121) a month, which sometimes rises to 18,000–20,000 taka ($145–$161) when she works overtime.

Her 15-year-old daughter and 12-year-old son dropped out of school earlier this year because she could not afford their education.

“We can barely afford one proper meal a day. This morning, we had only puffed rice and Bombay mix [a snack]. There was nothing for lunch. We’ve been going hungry, hoping to have a proper meal tonight. Yesterday was the same. This is how we survive now,” she told Al Jazeera.

“My son is so thin that you can count every rib in his chest. What else can I do?”

Begum is among approximately four million garment factory workers in Bangladesh, half of them women. They are now protesting for better wages .

Bangladesh, the world’s second-largest apparel exporter after China, is a key supplier to global fashion brands such as H&M, Zara, Levi Strauss, Walmart, and Primark. The country’s ready-made garment sector accounts for more ⁠than 80 percent of its export earnings, which touched $39bn last financial year.

Yet, the people sewing those clothes say their pay no longer covers basic living costs.

A Muslim-majority South Asian nation of 170 million people, Bangladesh has one of the world’s lowest wages among apparel-producing countries.

Cambodia has a minimum wage of $210 a month for garment workers, Vietnam’s range from $140-$210, while wages at China’s manufacturing hub of Guangdong range between $286 and $378.

That disparity – worsened by rising inflation and the growing cost of living – pushed the workers to strike and hit the streets on Saturday to demand a minimum wage of 30,000 taka ($241), more than double the current wage of 12,500 taka ($102).

On Sunday, Begum joined one such protest in the Jamgora part of the Ashulia industrial area on the outskirts of the capital Dhaka, with the police firing tear gas and stun grenades to disperse the protesters, and arresting dozens of them.

The ⁠Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association said the demonstrations disrupted operations at 529 factories on Sunday and affected nearly a million workers.

Later that day, the government announced the formation of a six-member wage board to review the workers’ demands.

But that did not stop the garment workers from returning to the streets for a third straight day on Monday.

In northern Dhaka’s Gazipur area, the workers blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway, and vandalised and torched several vehicles, while clashes with police were reported from the neighbouring Mirpur district.

“The government only makes promises,” Begum told Al Jazeera. “They haven’t told us when wages will increase and by how much.”

Rasel Khan, a 30-year-old garment worker at Ashulia, told Al Jazeera his monthly earnings of 18,000–20,000 taka ($145–$161), including overtime, were no longer enough to support his family, which included his mother and younger brother besides his wife and child.

As living costs soar, he has accumulated a debt of about 100,000 taka ($805) to meet his needs. “It’s impossible to support a family on this income anymore. Prices keep rising, and we have to borrow money just to survive,” he said.

The last revision of the minimum wage in the garment sector took place in December 2023. Since then, prices have continued to climb. Official data put annual inflation at 8.34 percent in September, including 7.22 percent for food and 9.30 percent for non-food expenses.

Begum says she pays 3,500 taka ($28) as rent for a single room shared with her mother and children. Her father, living in their village in the central district of Sirajganj, also depends on her income.

She says she is burning discarded paper and other materials to cook because she is not able to afford a gas cylinder that costs about 2,200 taka ($18).

Zahid Hussain, a former lead economist at the World Bank’s Dhaka office, said persistent inflation over the past five years has sharply eroded the purchasing power of low-paid workers.

“When real income falls, they have to cut their daily living standards,” he told Al Jazeera. “They don’t have any surplus income.”

Hussain said a recent hike in the salary of government employees has had a “demonstration effect” among private-sector workers waiting for a similar relief.

The government’s announcement of a wage board follows an amendment to labour laws to reduce the wage review cycle from five years to three years. The current three-year period ends in December.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman convened an emergency meeting of top government officials on Sunday, while Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed met the garment factory owners on Monday, assuring them that a new minimum wage would be fixed through negotiations.

Labour Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury meanwhile urged the workers to resume work, saying the wage board would begin its deliberations shortly.

But Babul Akhter, a workers’ representative on the board, called for the new wages to take effect with January 2027 salaries. He also asked the demonstrators to return to work and demanded the release of arrested workers and withdrawal of cases against them.

The impending wage negotiations come at a challenging time for Bangladesh’s garment industry, as manufacturers balance workers’ demands for better wages with rising production costs and intensifying global competition.

Sheikh Hossain Muhammad Mustafiz, an official at Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association and managing director of Cute Dress Industry Ltd, told Al Jazeera that fair wages and employment security must go hand in hand with their ability to compete in the international market.

“Workers deserve wages that support a decent standard of living. However, without fair purchasing prices from international brands, significant wage increases could put pressure on factories and threaten employment,” he said.

Mustafiz emphasised that protecting the workers’ purchasing power amid rising inflation is a responsibility that global brands that buy Bangladeshi garments must share.

“Sustainable wage growth cannot be achieved by manufacturers alone,” he said. “International brands must contribute through fair pricing and responsible purchasing practices to protect both the workers’ livelihoods and the industry’s long-term sustainability.”

Taqbir Huda, a Tech Global Institute senior fellow at the University of Oxford, accused the western brands who buy Bangladeshi garments of not addressing the issue of the workers’ rights.

“One party that could change the situation overnight has held the most extractive and exploitative role: the western buyer brands who hold the lion’s share of the value that is generated by the clothes that these workers produce,” he told Al Jazeera.

Huda said the wage board, which was due this year, was announced only after the workers began their protest.

“History gives very little reason for the workers to believe anything will improve unless they protest,” he said, adding that the formation of the wage board does not meet their demands unless it addresses rising inflation and the cost-of-living crisis.

For Begum, a drawn-out process to decide the new wages means another month of struggle to feed her family.

“Wages must rise, but food prices must also come down.”

articles.title: How a Harvard dream ended in tragedy for a Pakistani family
articles.summary: A 24-year-old physics graduate dies after her family pays millions to a man who lied about getting her into university.
articles.body:
Islamabad, Pakistan – The sign above the Rana Malik Center, a dairy shop in Islamabad’s G-10 neighbourhood, advertises milk, fresh yoghurt, lassi and desi ghee. Rana Muhammad Ijaz has lived with his family in the apartment above for more than three decades.

Sitting outside his shop in late October, Ijaz recalled how his youngest daughter, Laiba, would make tea for him every morning and then again at night before bedtime.

“She used to massage my shoulders before I went to bed too.” he told Al Jazeera.

Ijaz sat outside his shop, remembering her. “Now that she is gone, I miss it all.”

Laiba Ijaz, 24, a physics gold medallist from the publicly funded International Islamic University Islamabad (IIUI), was found dead near her home on October 9.

According to the initial findings of a police case, she likely died by suicide after she and her family were defrauded of millions of rupees – tens of thousands of dollars – by a man who promised her admission to Harvard University in the United States.

Muhammad Noman, accused of the fraud, was arrested two days later. He died on October 20 after being shot while in police custody. Police said his accomplices had opened fire to free him.

On October 21, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi visited the family and handed over more than 5 million rupees ($18,000) that officials said had been recovered from Noman.

But that money means little to Ijaz and his family. What mattered most – his daughter – is gone.

Ijaz studied until the eighth grade and his wife until grade 10, but all four of their daughters went to university.

Two of the sisters studied mathematics while one of Laiba’s elder sisters spent a year in China on a scholarship, learning Mandarin. Laiba, too, studied on scholarships, her father said, and won the gold medal at her university.

“The day she got it, Laiba danced and jumped in front of her sisters,” Ijaz said.

Laiba later taught science at an Islamabad school and gave out-of-school tuition classes to children between grades 2 and 6. IIUI offered her a scholarship to study in Saudi Arabia, but she wanted to pursue higher studies in the US, her father said.

She asked him to pay for her studies abroad.

“’I did all the work myself, and I teach tuitions too, so can’t you do this for me?'” she asked her father, he recalled.

He told her: “My dear daughter, I will.”

“From there, we started preparing,” Ijaz said.

Then they met Noman, and the dream grew. Unknown to the family at the time, it was built on hollow promises and outright lies.

Laiba met Noman this year at a call centre where she worked in Islamabad’s Blue Area, the capital’s main business district. Her hours were late, and most of her colleagues were male. Ijaz was uncomfortable with Laiba’s work environment and encouraged her to leave. She quit the job.

But Noman then began coming to the shop to buy milk and yoghurt. During his visits, Ijaz said, he asked about Laiba’s plans to study in Saudi Arabia.

“No, we will not go to Saudi Arabia. We will go to America,” Ijaz said he told Noman.

Noman claimed to work at the Supreme Court, showed Ijaz a service card and said he needed no licence because he was a government employee.

“The card looked right to me too. I showed it to the people next to me,” Ijaz said.

Noman offered to help Laiba with her application. Ijaz and Laiba decided to accept his offer. “That was our biggest mistake,” the father said.

The family paid in stages, starting with 2.2 million rupees ($7,900) for university fees, Ijaz said. Noman later claimed Harvard needed a statement proving 7.2 million rupees ($25,900) in funds, which he insisted had to pass through his account to be converted into dollars.

“To help my daughter, I sold a plot which I owned. I also sold the [family] jewellery, so I could complete the demanded 7.2 million rupees,” he said.

Documents shared with Al Jazeera appear to trace a real application: Harvard offer and scholarship letters, a US immigration form with an official-looking stamp, a sponsor’s affidavit from a New York relative, an embassy record bearing Laiba’s photograph and a business-class ticket to Boston.

The final file, handed over in late September, also contained a bank statement in Laiba’s name and an October 12 visa interview date, Ijaz said.

In early October, Ijaz said he called Noman to help prepare his daughter for the interview. Noman told him he was in Quetta and would return the next day.

Suspicious of his evasiveness, the family showed the documents to a travel agent and discovered the Boston ticket was fake.

A lawyer neighbour checked the file and told them none of the documents was genuine. They learned the truth about October 6, Ijaz said.

The family was shattered. “I used to tell her, ‘What had to happen has happened,'” Ijaz said.

But Laiba “continued to have hope” that US authorities and Harvard might still process a real application on her behalf, Ijaz said.

On October 9 as Ijaz prepared to close his shop for Friday prayers, Laiba told him Noman had sent her a message. He would pray at their area mosque and then come to see the family.

“Laiba, my dear, he will not come. There is no need to listen to his message,” Ijaz recalled telling her. It was one of the last things he said to his daughter.

He told Laiba to stay inside and asked his wife to ensure she did. When he returned, his wife said Laiba had received a message from Noman and left despite her mother’s protestations.

“Upon hearing this, the ground slipped from under my feet,” Ijaz said.

Ijaz sent Laiba’s brother-in-law, Zaid bin Afzal, and one of Laiba’s younger brothers to search for her. One of Laiba’s sisters, meanwhile, guided them by using an app that helped them trace the missing woman’s phone to an area near the house.

They found her body about 3:30pm, less than two hours after Laiba had left home. Zaid called the police emergency number and then rang his father-in-law, asking him to come to the spot urgently. He didn’t want to tell Ijaz about Laiba’s death on the phone, so he told his father-in-law that Laiba was “being stubborn and refusing to come home”.

But Ijaz instantly sensed something was wrong. When he reached the spot, he found his daughter dead.

Laiba was among a growing number of Pakistanis hoping to study in the US.

During the 2024-2025 school year, more than 13,000 Pakistani students were enrolled at US institutions, a 75 percent increase from 2017-2018, according to the Institute of International Education’s Open Doors report.

The Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) said Noman was not a registered visa agent. The government also has left a gaping hole in the market for foreign studies: It does not regulate education consultancies, according to the industry body All Pakistan Association of Foreign Education and Immigration Consultants.

“I do not know of a regulatory body that checks or registers education consultants,” Nushmiya Sukhera, cofounder of CollegeWorks, a college consultancy in Lahore, told Al Jazeera.

“No education consultancy can guarantee admission,” she said.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif ordered Noman’s arrest a day after Laiba died. Police and the FIA registered separate cases.

Police said on October 20 that four men on two motorcycles opened fire as Noman was being taken to recover evidence. The men, according to the police, were trying to help Noman escape, but ended up shooting him. Noman, they said, died while being treated for his bullet wounds.

To Ijaz, Noman’s death, however controversial the circumstances, represents a modicum of justice. “In my view, whatever happened was right,” the father said, of the agent’s killing. Authorities are investigating the attack on Noman, but no one has been arrested yet.

Meanwhile, a senior police official, speaking to Al Jazeera on condition of anonymity, said investigations into Laiba’s death were ongoing.

Initial postmortem findings pointed to suicide, the official said, adding that footage showed Laiba leaving home on her own with a phone in her hand.

The remaining forensic report usually takes 15 to 20 days, the official said.

But Ijaz and his family refuse to accept that Laiba died by suicide.

Zaid said after discovering Laiba that “she could not have done this herself”.

“She did not die herself,” he said. “He [Noman] killed her.”

articles.title: Lake District farm fears campsite ban could damage business
articles.summary: The Lake District National Park Authority wants to tighten rules around pop-up campsites.
articles.body:
A farmer fears plans to tighten rules for pop-up campsites in a national park could spell the end of her business.

The Lake District National Park Authority (LDNPA) wants to make it compulsory for temporary campsites to require planning permission. Current rules allow sites operating for fewer than 60 days to be set up by simply notifying the authority.

Ruby Cardiff runs Newlands Valley Campsite, near Keswick, during the summer to supplement income from her Keskadale Farm. She said the ban would "strip away a crucial source of income" from farmers who depend on diversification "for their survival".

The LDNPA said the proposal aimed to "prevent unneighbourly or harmful sites".

Cardiff started using one of her fields as a pop-up site after the coronavirus pandemic, when travel bans meant more people holidayed in the UK.

She said the site's popularity helped her business plug the gap left by the phasing out of EU funding following Brexit.

"This has been absolutely perfect for us because obviously it's just seasonal so it doesn't take away from our other farming operations, we can still lamb and we can still have cows in the winter, because obviously there's only so much we can do."

Cardiff said when she tried applying for permission to run the campsite for up to 80 days to have more flexibility in operations, the LDNPA turned down the proposal because of the visual impact on the landscape.

She said: "We live in the valley, we live in the Lake District, there's fells all around us so the visual impact, we were never going to mitigate that, so we could never get around it."

If plans to ban pop-up campsite are confirmed following the LDNPA consultation, Cardiff said she feared she would not get planning permission again.

"It could be the end of our business and many other businesses."

Data from Pitchup.com, a campsite booking service, showed pop-up campsites in Cumbria generated about £1.6m in revenue this year, with a further £800,000 being spent in local businesses such as pubs, shops and attractions.

Cardiff has launched a petition opposing the LDNPA's proposal, which garnered hundreds of signatures.

Those in favour of pop-up campsites argue they help to deal with the Lake District's popularity and tackle issues such as fly camping .

However, critics have said the unregulated nature of them means residents are left to deal with potential problems such as noise, anti-social behaviour and impacts on the environment alone.

Bowness-on-Windermere resident Sarah Wilson campaigned with neighbours for the LDNPA to tighten rules .

She said the campaign asked for "the same planning scrutiny as everyone else" and sought to protect the national park, which is a Unesco World Heritage site.

"What we don't want to do is create pop-up campsites that damage the very environment that these visitors are coming to see."

She said she was in favour of farms diversifying, but oversight was needed to ensure heritage and landscape protections were in place.

"We're just trying to make sure that the Lake District National Park is kept as beautiful as it is already."

The LDNPA's head of development management Andrew Smith said greater control of pop-up sites would help manage problems.

"Many temporary recreational campsites are well operated, but they can also be poorly sited and have negative impacts – for example there is currently no minimum separation required between a permitted development campsite and a neighbour's house."

He added a consultation on the proposal was open until 16 November and any comments were welcome.

articles.title: Law to be changed for Holly Newton, teen murdered by ex-boyfriend
articles.summary: The family of Holly Newton, stabbed to death at 15, is told the law will change after their campaigning.
articles.body:
The family of a murdered schoolgirl says the government has told them it plans to create a new law defining teenage abusive relationships – because of their campaigning.

Micala and Lee Trussler met the Safeguarding and Violence Against Women and Girls minister Satvir Kaur at the Home Office in London on Monday, where they were given an outline of the plans.

Their daughter, Holly Newton, was 15 when she was stabbed to death in an alleyway in Hexham in January 2023.

She was killed by her ex-boyfriend Logan MacPhail, who was 16 at the time and could not accept the relationship was over. He had been controlling and stalked Holly in the run up to her death.

Police recorded her murder as knife crime because the law does not recognise those under 16 as victims of domestic violence.

This is something her mum and stepdad, Micala and Lee Trussler, have been campaigning to change.

Lee said: "Without that classification they can't receive the help and guidance that they need to safely exit that relationship."

But Micala and Lee agree that a standalone definition for abuse in teenage relationships would be as effective as lowering the age someone can be classed as a victim of domestic abuse.

Micala said: "I think a stand alone definition is actually better than just lowering the age because it is actually giving teenagers better protection and also acknowledging teenage relationships can look a lot different to adult relationships.

"We've definitely felt really proud that we've got here because we have campaigned for so long. It's also quite emotional because we've still lost Holly.

"But I do feel like they've [the government] taken Holly's story seriously and they've realised the failings in her case. And we're now helping other young people get the support they really, really need."

In January, a House of Lords select committee started a review of the Domestic Abuse Act 2021 to consider its impact and effectiveness.

Among the areas it examined was the definition of domestic abuse and The Act's recognition of children – like Holly - as victims. The move to explore a new definition for teenage relationship abuse comes as a result of this review.

In a statement the Safeguarding and Violence Against Women and Girls Minister Satvir Kaur said: "Micala Trussler has shown incredible courage in campaigning in Holly's memory, following the unimaginable loss of her daughter.

"Stories like Holly's are why we are deploying the full power of the state to halve violence against women and girls in a decade."

The MP for Hexham Joe Morris who accompanied the Trusslers to see the minister said the government was taking the family's concerns seriously.

He said: "This is a major victory for Micala and her hard work and campaigning on this issue because Holly was failed, and I'm delighted to see the seriousness and the rigour the government is treating this issue, and I think it's a massive step in the right direction to get Holly's law on the statute book."

The government has not revealed a timeline for the proposals or said when the full review of the Domestic Abuse Act 2021 will be revealed.

Logan MacPhail was detained for at least 17 years in 2024 for carrying out the "vicious and brutal" stabbing.

articles.title: Firework displays cancelled over concerns about wildlife and pets
articles.summary: Displays by a college and primary school are cancelled after concerns for the welfare of wildlife and pets.
articles.body:
Some fireworks displays have been cancelled over concerns for the welfare of local wildlife and pets.

National Star College, near Cheltenham, Gloucestershire, said they had cancelled their fireworks event after a nearby sanctuary expressed fears for the birds in their care being rehabilitated.

A local display organised by parents at Upton St Leonards Primary School was also cancelled after some residents raised concerns about horses in a nearby field.

Chief executive for National Star College, Lynette Barrett, said going forward the college would be looking for "quieter, more environmentally friendly alternatives to classic firework displays".

It comes as the government has just finished a consultation on cutting the noise of fireworks sold to the public , with concerns raised by the National Farmers' Union (NFU) over the distress caused to animals .

Russell's Rescue is a volunteer-run rescue, rehabilitation and sanctuary for crows and has been been based at Ullenwood, near National Star College, since January.

Helen Motteram, who runs the centre, said they had not been aware of the annual fireworks display until they saw recent social media posts and contacted the college about their concerns.

"When birds are in an aviary, they can't escape. We've had it before where the birds panic and they fly into the mesh, either killing or injuring themselves," she said.

"We've just released around 33 birds and a lot of them are still nesting nearby, so you can imagine that is going to be pretty traumatic for them."

Although Barrett said the students were disappointed, she added National Star College was focused on finding a way to celebrate the occasion that kept the environment and local wildlife safe.

"What we don't want to do is replace the fireworks display with something that's equally environmentally problematic," she said.

Motteram has also expressed a desire to work with the college and offered to give an educational talk for the students.

In Upton St Leonards, some residents were against a display organised by the local Parent Teacher Association. Due to take place on Sunday, it was due to be a "low noise" display to raise funds for the school playground.

Organisers wrote on a community page: "A low-noise display was chosen specifically to protect local animals, and be inclusive of those children who find loud events overwhelming, with the potential added benefit to reduce the number of private garden displays across and around the village.

"We gave 10 weeks' notice and invited direct feedback, proactively engaging with the responses we received, and spending weeks consulting equine charities to make the event work for everyone."

They added: "Sadly, despite our efforts we have exhausted every option to move forward."

articles.title: Southampton Airport plans to expand passenger terminal
articles.summary: Airport says there are fewer planes, but airlines use larger aircraft carrying more passengers.
articles.body:
An airport could be expanded to handle planes carrying almost three times as many passengers under new plans.

Southampton Airport has drawn up plans for an 800 sq m (8611 sq ft) extension to its passenger terminal in Mitchell Way, Eastleigh, alongside changes to the internal layout.

AGS Airports, which owns the airport, said the extra space is needed because airlines are now operating larger aircraft carrying around 200 passengers, rather than 70-seater planes.

The airport operator said this change has reduced the number of aircraft movements but created a need for more space inside the terminal due to passenger boarding.

Under the current system, up to 200 passengers may need to wait in a controlled pre-boarding area for around 15 minutes so they can board quickly once the arriving passengers have left the aircraft.

The proposed extension would be built on an area known as Stand 6, next to the existing terminal building.

AGS Airports said it has asked Eastleigh Borough Council to confirm if the works can be carried out under permitted development rights.

It forms part of plans to further improve Southampton Airport, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.

Rather than seeking conventional planning permission, the airport has applied for a Lawful Development Certificate confirming that the extension can go ahead under existing permitted development rights.

Speaking on the proposals, councillor Steve Broomfield, who sits on the council's airport consultative committee, welcomed the idea.

He said: "It enables the airport to be better able to process modern, more environmentally efficient aircraft and the resulting increase in passenger numbers."

Documents stated that the original terminal, dating from 1994, covers 6,176 square metres and has previously been extended by 124 square metres.

A public consultation will run until 18 November and a decision is due by 10 December.

articles.body: MUMBAI: Mumbai Police have launched a parallel investigation into the alleged network of mule bank accounts being used to route funds generated through online gaming, betting and cyber fraud activities, with investigators examining the financial trail and the alleged role of individuals named in a recent complaint, including Samundar Singh Rathod and Mukesh Jain.The parallel probe comes amid an ongoing Enforcement Directorate (ED) investigation into the alleged online betting network linked to All Panel Exchange (APX) and MGM91.The ED has been examining the use of mule bank accounts, shell companies and payment intermediaries to collect and layer proceeds generated through online betting and cyber fraud.Sources said Mumbai police have began investigation as many of these mule accounts identified by the ED are common in their investigations.The city crime branch has busted a major international cyber fraud and money laundering syndicate, arresting 12 members who were allegedly operating from a sea-facing villa in Calangute, Goa.Investigators suspect the syndicate laundered more than Rs 500 crore of cyber fraud proceeds to handlers based in Dubai using mule bank accounts and SIM cards.The parallel Mumbai Police investigation could help establish the local banking and operational links of the alleged network, while the ED continues to investigate the suspected money-laundering trail.A complaint filed by activist Santosh Gholap before eight central agencies has sought a detailed financial investigation into the alleged network and named Rathod and Jain, among others.The complaint has alleged that several bank accounts and UPI IDs were being used to facilitate betting transactions and route funds through multiple entities.Mumbai Police are examining the alleged use of bank accounts as conduits for online gaming and betting transactions, including the movement of funds through multiple accounts and the identities of the actual beneficiaries.The investigation is expected to focus on the account holders, operators facilitating the transactions and the financial links between different entities.According to the complaint, mule accounts were allegedly operated through small offices in Mumbai, Pune, Goa, Delhi and Bengaluru. It has also sought scrutiny of 17 bank accounts and 46 individuals, besides claiming to possess details of around 20,442 casino players.The ED, meanwhile, had conducted searches at 20 premises across Mumbai, Pune, Mehsana, Surat and Hyderabad on October 13 as part of its money-laundering investigation.The agency has found that more than 200 shell and front companies were allegedly onboarded through Pune-based Edsom Fintech's iPaisa payment platform to facilitate transactions linked to online betting and cyber fraud operators.Investigators suspect that funds were routed through multiple mule accounts before being transferred through disguised trade transactions, cash withdrawals and cryptocurrency channels.Edsom Fintech founder Ram U Ramdhani has been arrested in the case.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: Two former partners' fight over a Sausalito house led to a legal-fee demand of $90,010; a California federal judge has now ordered one to pay the other $66,192.50 after a partially successful court motion
articles.summary: A dispute over a shared home can continue long after a relationship ends, particularly when disagreements over property ownership turn into lengthy legal
articles.body: A dispute over a shared home can continue long after a relationship ends, particularly when disagreements over property ownership turn into lengthy legal proceedings. In Sausalito, California, a former couple's fight over a house led to a separate dispute over attorney fees after one partner partly succeeded in getting allegations against him struck from a lawsuit. The legal battle took another turn when he sought $90,010 from his former partner to cover his legal expenses. In its October 30, 2026, order in Fotsch v. Shroder, available in Justia, the US District Court for the Northern District of California granted the request in part, ordering Mackenzie Fotsch to pay Matthew Shroder $66,192.50 while rejecting his demand for additional, unspecified fees.Dispute centred on a Sausalito propertyMackenzie Fotsch and Matthew Shroder, who were formerly in a romantic relationship, became involved in litigation concerning a house in Sausalito. Their dispute included an unlawful-detainer action that Shroder had filed and pursued against Fotsch. Fotsch subsequently brought claims against Shroder, including allegations involving contract disputes, unjust enrichment, breach of fiduciary duty and conversion. Shroder responded with a special motion to strike under California's anti-SLAPP law.The law protects people from lawsuits targeting their exercise of constitutionally protected rights, including participation in legal proceedings. Shroder argued that certain allegations in Fotsch's complaint relied on his protected litigation activities. The court partly agreed, striking portions of four allegations to the extent that they made his filing, service and prosecution of the unlawful-detainer action a basis for liability. Those allegations could remain in the complaint as background and evidence. However, it refused to dismiss the entire claims and allowed the unjust-enrichment claim to proceed.Shroder sought $90,010 in legal expensesFollowing his partial success, Shroder sought attorney fees and costs under California's anti-SLAPP statute, which allows a defendant who prevails on a special motion to strike to recover reasonable legal expenses. His application totalled $90,010. This included $45,685 for the anti-SLAPP motion, $40,720 for preparing and arguing the subsequent attorney-fee motion, and $3,605 in Westlaw legal research charges. He also requested additional fees that might arise later.The application covered work by three lawyers and a paralegal, whose hourly rates ranged from $225 to $900. Fotsch challenged the amount, arguing that Shroder had achieved only limited success because the court had allowed her claims to survive. She also questioned the billing records, the hours claimed and the expenses associated with preparing the fee application. She proposed limiting the award to $3,593, or at most $7,129.50, based on the portions of the anti-SLAPP motion that had succeeded. She also opposed the research charges and the request for unspecified future fees.Court reduced the claimed attorney feesThe judge recognised that Shroder had not secured everything he requested. The court had rejected his attempt to strike entire claims and had allowed the unjust-enrichment claim to continue. However, it found that removing the unlawful-detainer proceedings as a basis for liability and damages had materially narrowed the issues in the lawsuit.Rather than calculating fees solely according to the proportion of allegations struck, the court deducted time associated with unsuccessful portions of the motion. It also removed an hour spent correcting an over-length reply brief. The court consequently approved $40,887.50 in attorney fees for the anti-SLAPP proceedings. It allowed the full $3,605 in Westlaw research expenses, finding that the charges were supported by itemised records and related to the legal issues.The judge separately examined the $40,720 requested for preparing the attorney-fee motion. The work involved 66.8 hours, including 63.4 hours by the principal drafter, nearly twice the 33.9 hours he had spent drafting the original anti-SLAPP motion. The court considered this excessive. It also noted that parts of the application repeated arguments already decided and included discussions of the lawyers' professional backgrounds and criticism of opposing counsel. The court therefore reduced the principal lawyer's claimed time by 50 per cent, bringing the recoverable fees for the fee application to $21,700.Final award fixed at $66,192.50The court ordered Fotsch to pay Shroder $62,587.50 in attorney fees, comprising $40,887.50 for the anti-SLAPP proceedings and $21,700 for the fee application. An additional $3,605 was allowed for legal research costs. The judge rejected Shroder's request for further, unquantified attorney fees, requiring any additional expenses to be specified and supported. The October 30 order resolves the attorney-fee dispute, not the underlying disagreement over the Sausalito property. Fotsch's remaining claims were not dismissed, and the ruling does not determine the ultimate outcome of the former partners' wider legal battle.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Devon charity warns about damage caused by over-foraging fungi
articles.summary: It says over-foraging, particularly in protected areas, damages habitats and wildlife.
articles.body:
The impacts of over-foraging natural spaces, particularly in protected areas, can damage habitats, a Devon charity has said.

The Woodland Trust said unsustainable harvesting of plants - and particularly fungi - could put wildlife under pressure.

Joe Middleton, site manager for the Woodland Trust, said he had seen commercial mushroom pickers "wiping out everything on the path edges they can find".

Under Section 4 of the Theft Act 1968, it is "perfectly legal to forage for fruit, foliage, flowers, and fungi on any land, provided they are wild and collected strictly for personal use", but "foraging becomes criminal theft if you pick wild plants for commercial sale or reward without permission".

Middleton said: "I have seen commercial pickers, dropped off in mini buses with bags for life, laden heavy with mushrooms and they are going through and they are wiping out everything on the path edges they can find, trampling the forest floor."

The majority of mushrooms are not edible to humans, so picking them can be potentially dangerous.

In the autumn they are an essential source of food for animals such as deer and badgers, all the way down to things that live in the soil such as worms and woodlice.

Middleton said: "If we start decimating the population, it takes their food source away.

"They can't just get up and move, a lot of our wildlife is dependent on this fungi. We just need to be a bit more sustainable in what we are doing."

Entering private property without a landowner's consent to forage is a civil rather than criminal offence. However, foraging is heavily restricted or illegal in local Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs) or protected areas like Woodland Trust sites.

Using ingredients from local areas is very fashionable on social media at the moment.

John Dobson, from the Refectory restaurant near Ugborough, said he thought there were other factors too.

He said: "The rising cost of ingredients; they're getting really, really expensive, so I think that could be encouraging people to go out and source things from other places. There is also a lack of education about the impact."

Dobson added he made sure to forage responsibly, only taking a third of what he found, and doing so with any landowner's permission.

Middleton said foraging was a great way to connect with nature, but he wanted to encourage people to enjoy woodlands without taking any of it home with them too.

He said: "We've gone a long way from Victorian times in terms of taking everything we see and pinning it and netting it.

"Now we are in a technological age. We can just use our phones, take great pictures; we can look without touching - particularly in a protected place."
